Live injury updates

Two star players who have each missed the past two weeks were back at practice for their respective teams.

The Philadelphia Eagles welcomed back Saquon Barkley after he's been out since Week 4 due to a hamstring injury. If all goes well, the running back is in line to play when the Eagles host the Dallas Cowboys on "Monday Night Football."

Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson was also back on the practice field after sitting two games with an ankle injury. He was limited for a second straight day on Thursday, but took part in drills ahead of Sunday's game against the Cincinnati Bengals.

There was a worrying sign for the Los Angeles Rams on Thursday as wide receiver Puka Nacua left practice with a calf injury. He was listed as limited three days before the Rams, who will already be without wideout Davante Adams (hamstring), face the Las Vegas Raiders.

Nacua has already missed two games this season with a psoas injury.

Other Week 7 injuries to monitor:

  • San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Mike Evans (ribs/Achilles) and defensive end Nick Bosa (knee/calf) did not practice on Thursday. Bosa has not practiced for almost a month after pulling his calf in practice and has already missed four games with the injury.

  • New York Jets running back Breece Hall (quad) returned to practice on Thursday. While he was a limited participant, it's an encouraging sign for Hall, who has missed three games with the injury.

  • The Arizona Cardinals are not expecting to have Jeremiyah Love (ankle) available to them this week against the Denver Broncos. The running back will reportedly be sidelined for a second straight game. Head coach Mike LaFleur told the media last week that an injured reserve stint had not been discussed for Love.

  • Baker Mayfield (thumb) could return this week for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The quarterback has been out since injuring the digit in Week 3. He returned to practice on Wednesday and head coach Todd Bowles said he wants to see what Mayfield looks like on Friday before making a decision on his availability for Sunday's game against the Carolina Panthers. Whoever is at quarterback for Tampa this week may not have wideout Emeka Egbuka, who is in concussion protocol.

  • While the Houston Texans likely won't have running back David Montgomery (groin) against the New York Giants, they will be getting back Tank Dell. The wide receiver has not played since suffering a serious knee injury in Dec. 2024. Nearly 22 months later, the 2023 third-round draft pick said he's feeling back to his old self. "I'm anxious to get back out there and play some football," he said.

item.title: NFL predictions: 4 game picks for pivotal Chiefs-Seahawks matchup
item.description: Will Kenneth Walker get revenge against the Seahawks? Will Zach Charbonnet provide a spark for Seattle’s offense? Let’s make some picks!
item.content:encoded:
Sunday Night Football brings the Kansas City Chiefs to Seattle for a Week 7 matchup, also unofficially known as the “Kenneth Walker III Bowl.” If you’re looking for player props and game-day value, check out the latest lines at FanDuel Sportsbook before kickoff. 

The Seattle Seahawks are coming off of two straight losses and are staring a sub .500 record straight in the eyes. The Chiefs meanwhile are undefeated and are currently elated with their recent running back signing (and Offensive Player of the Year candidate) Kenneth Walker III. Let’s look at some game picks ahead of this matchup Sunday Night. 

Kenneth Walker III over 84.5 rushing yards (-114)

    I know Walker III is not a Seahawk anymore. However, considering his dominance this season, and the Seahawks lack of dominant running game, this is surely the game pick on the top of everyone’s mind. Walker III is averaging 133 yards per game this season. Meanwhile the Seahawks defense has not allowed a 100 yard rusher in a franchise record, 35 games – not since October 27, 2024. One of these juggernauts will have to break in this matchup. 

    The betting line being at 84.5 seems to be lower than many expected, or at least lower than I expected. Walker III is on a career heater right now. His ability to flip the field at any moment and break any run into a house call is very rare. Even if the Seahawks defense holds Walker III in check, it only takes one explosive run to get close to this 84.5 line. On top of this, Walker III already gets a large share of carries, and is now facing a revenge game. I would expect Walker III to get a ton of carries in this game, which means tons of opportunities to hit this line. All of this considered, it is tough to see Walker III not being able to hit at least 85 yards rushing. That doesn’t mean that he will break 100 yards – the Seahawks could still very easily extend their streak to 36 games. However, this will be their hardest challenge yet. 

    The pick: Kenneth Walker III over 84.5 rushing yards. 

    Over 42.5 points (-112) 

      The line for this game is 42.5, also a little lower. The Seahawks have scored at least 29 points four times this season. Their only two games where they scored less was in Week 1 with Drew Lock coming in with no first team reps, and in Week 6 with a short week Thursday Night Football game. 

      Add to this, the fact that the Seahawks are playing the red hot Kenneth Walker III and the Chiefs. There is a good chance that the Seahawks offense will need to keep up with Kansas City and their elite running game. That will surely be easier to do with Anthony Bradford and Zach Charbonnet likely returning for this game. Expect a high scoring affair in the battle of former AFC West foes. 

      The pick: Over 42.5 total points (-112). 

      Jaxon Smith-Njigba over 92.5 receiving yards (-114).

        Leading the NFL in receptions (49), receiving yards (717), and receiving touchdowns (7), JSN is once again on a heater. JSN has only missed the receiving yards line once this season – week 4 against the Los Angeles Chargers where he put up only 76 yards (18.5 yards shy of the line). 

        With the Seahawks run game struggling, and Sam Darnold looking less confident week in and week out, expect the safety blanket, JSN to have another big game this week against the Chiefs. Despite averaging 143.4 yards per game, the lines still remain fairly low. With it this low, the smartest move would be to bet the over. 

        The pick: Jaxon Smith-Njigba over 92.5 receiving yards. 

        Zach Charbonnet to score 2+ touchdowns  (+750) 

          The first three picks may not be too risky. However, this last pick is very risky. Trying to correctly guess who will score two or more touchdowns is a Hail Mary of sorts, but why not live on the edge? Charbonnet, who was just activated off of the PUP list, is expected to make his season debut against the Chiefs. 

          This season, the Seahawks have struggled in short yardage situations. That is exactly where Charbonnet’s return is huge. When on the field, Charbonnet tends to find the end zone. Last season, Charbonnet led the Seahawks with 12 touchdowns. The year prior, Charbonnet had 8 touchdowns. Although this will be his first game back since tearing his ACL in the 2025 playoffs, look to see Charbonnet get these opportunities once again. It isn’t just the short yardage situations however. Charbonnet is also a strong pass catcher and gives the Seahawks an opportunity to score as a receiver as well. Despite only having one career receiving touchdown, Charbonnet still has 95 receptions for 693 yards in his young three year career.

          The other elephant in the room with Charbonnet’s return is Kenneth Walker III’s absence. Throughout his career Charbonnet has always split the backfield with Walker III. However, this season Charbonnet has an opportunity to prove he is the clear number one running back. With Jadarian Price still on injured reserve, and the other running backs on the roster proving lackluster, this week will be a perfect opportunity for Charbonnet to prove he can lead this backfield. 

          The pick: Zach Charbonnet to score 2+ touchdowns.

item.title: Unknown rookie could be key to the Rams’ ailing defensive line
item.description: Practice squad behemoth Bill Norton has the girth to be a space eater
item.content:encoded:
As the Los Angeles Rams scramble to assemble a new defensive line in the wake of injuries to both Kobie Turner and Poona Ford, undrafted rookie Bill Norton could be the answer that Chris Shula is looking for. Although Norton is on the practice squad and yet to be called up for an NFL game, there are components to his player profile that make him a more intriguing option moving forward than L.A.’s current stable of backups.

Rams fans just want something to be excited about right now, and an underdog story like Norton’s fits the bill.

What went wrong this season?

Injury attrition continues to take its toll on the Rams defensive line with this weeks news that Poona Ford (torn tricep) is lost for the season and Kobie Turner faces extended time, a minimum of four weeks, on the the Injured Reserve List. Both L.A.’s coaching and front office braintrust are left scrambling to fill the void.

The Rams just happen to have a prospect on their practice squad that is certainly big enough to take up some of that space: 6’ 5” 330 lb. defensive tackle Bill Norton.

In the recent past, the Rams have been trending towards smaller, speaking relatively when it’s 300 lb. men, defensive interior players that can be moved freely across the front line. Norton’s thick and wide frame breaks that mold. Now in the midst of his second season, he signed with the Rams as an undrafted free agent in the spring of 2025. At that time, his addition appeared to be another piece of L.A.’s big picture plan to improve a run defense that had a Bottom 10 NFL ranking in 2024. Norton has not seen any time on the 53-man roster and has been biding his time toiling on the L.A. practice squad

Norton boasts a good pedigree. Originally recruited and signed by the Georgia Bulldogs as a four-star high school recruit. Played basketball, as well. Spent four seasons with the “Dawgs and was part of two National Championship teams. He never was able to break through in Athens, playing in 26 games and accumulating modest stats (12 tackles, 3.5 for loss) on special teams and in a reserve role. Rode the portal west to Arizona for 2023 and had his best college season, starting 12 of 13 games and charting 32 tackles, 2.5 for loss, three batted down passes and two forced fumbles. Norton stepped in class for his final season in 2024 with the Texas Longhorns. He saw action in 14 games and claimed 14 tackles, 1.5 for loss, and one sack.

Finding a role that fits

Gone are are the days when L.A. made due with a predominant five-man front base. Sub packages are now the rule, based mostly on four man defensive fronts. Last year, according to Sharp Football Analysis, the Rams used sub defensive packages at a 75 percent rate. In the past two seasons they have moved towards a deep rotation on the defensive interior, at times using as many as seven different players in a game, and moving them interchangeably. Norton will find his fit as one of those pieces, 

Norton projects best into the Poona Ford role, as the dirty work guy tasked with clogging the inside gaps, disrupting run lanes and absorbing double team blocks to open things up for others. Not glamorous, the job is for lunch pail-type players that don’t need glossy stat counts to keep them pounding away. There might also be place for him on special teams, he was a regular performer on those units in college. Georgia Bulldogs head coach Kirby Smart said of his special teams efforts,

“What a great kid man, this guy worked his tail off here, worked really hard. One of his key roles was with special teams, he played on our field goal protection unit and was the best at doing it.”

What does the film say?

With the Rams strategy of all roster contributors sitting out the preseason, it creates the opportunity to see a lot of Norton on film. L.A. did not limit him to nose tackle or shading the center in the A gaps, he was employed up and down the front line. On field goal/extra point protection, he displayed a low pad level and wide base and staying connected (no open lanes) to the players on his flanks.

He’s not an explosive gap shooter/penetrator that will create pass rush pressure. Nor does he have a toolbox full of moves that he can combine to wreak havoc. Norton is going to use linear push as his predominant move. If he gets stymied, he’s aware of getting into passing lanes and stretching out his frame to tighten passing lanes. He had three batted passes in preseason. Not often, but he had a few reps from outside on the edge, and the short runway allowed him to do a pretty good job using a direct speed to power attack.

Inside, taking on blockers is where he’ll have the best chance for success. While arm length is just adequate (32 1/4”) and his punch isn’t of stun grade, he does a good job of landing first and is quite accurate. It enables him to keep good control tostack/shed blockers. When you combine the extension with a wide base, he was able to hold ground against double teams at the preseason level of competition. Not gifted with plus agility or change of direction skills, but he moves laterally pretty well for his girth. More importantly, Norton is a hustler, navigates well in traffic,  and takes good angles in pursuit. Although he’ll likely struggle in the open field, expect him get his share of hustle stops from behind, even across the field.

Does Bill Norton offer any value?

The Rams put a lot of weight on the shoulders of the defensive line. In the past, along with run-stopping responsibilities, the front (including edges in this case) has been expected to provide pass rush pressure without a lot of blitz calls. Although the Rams are blitzing at a 10% higher rate this year than last (27.5% to 17.7%), it’s not identity of the defense. Norton shouldn’t be expected to upgrade the pass rush, maybe clean up and/or back door hustle pursuit

Fans have to be realistic about the value Norton can offer. He is not an All-Pro waiting for his big chance and bringing a polished game up with him from the practice squad. What he can offer is rotational snaps, particularly working in running situations. Providing a big body to help improve  L.A.’s between the tackles run defense. Every double team he can draw and engage will keep a linebacker/safety clean to fill a lane or give one of the better-equipped pass rushers a 1on1.

On the defensive interior, big problems demand big answers. Bill Norton certainly offers the size, will the Rams apply it?

item.title: AFC North Preview, Week 7: Bengals and Ravens face off in high-stakes matchup
item.description: Previewing every AFC North team’s matchup in Week 7
item.content:encoded:
Updated Standings:

  1. Cleveland Browns 4-2
  2. Pittsburgh Steelers 4-2
  3. Baltimore Ravens 4-2
  4. Cincinnati Bengals 3-2
Pittsburgh Steelers

Matchup: @ New Orleans Saints (London), 9:30am EST

The Steelers are traveling to London this week as the “road” team in a matchup with the New Orleans Saints — making them the second AFC North squad to play internationally this season. Last week, Pittsburgh escaped Tampa Bay with an overtime victory, their first consecutive win of the year, and improved to 4-2. The Steelers have scored 24+ points in four straight games after a slow offensive start in the first two weeks.

Against the Saints, the Steelers have a good chance to continue their scoring momentum. New Orleans is giving up 377.7 yards per game, fourth most in the NFL, and their allowing 29.7 points per game — tied for the worst mark. The Saints have been particularly vulnerable defending the run. Jaylen Warren’s production came back to earth in Week 5, but Rico Dowdle returned and was efficient with 40 yards on seven carries. The Steelers ran the ball only 22 times compared to 49 passes, so expect them to strike more balance in this game.

Defensively, the Steelers will need to key in on slowing down star wide receiver Chris Olave — who ranks second in the NFL in receiving yards (580) and fourth in receptions (43). The Saints’ passing attack was prolific through Weeks 1-4 but has taken a step back over the last two games. The Steelers should be able to hold the Saints in check on the ground, though, so prevent quarterback Tyler Shough from making big plays remains the priority.

Baltimore Ravens

Matchup:vs. Cincinnati Bengals, 1:00pm EST

Coming off a loss to the Browns, the Ravens are now trying to avoid a damaging 0-2 divisional record when they host the Bengals this Sunday. Baltimore’s Lamar Jackson-less offense regressed significantly last week. The Ravens scored 10 points within the first few minutes of the game and were shut out from there. Whether or not Jackson returns to action this week remains the biggest storyline and determining factor for the Ravens’ chances of winning.

Regardless of whether he’s back or Tyler Huntley is starting again, the Ravens’ offensive line will need to have their best game of the season. The Bengals’ defensive front poses challenges, particularly on the interior with star defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence. Cam Jurgens, whom the Ravens recently acquired via trade, is set to make his first start with the team at center and will be immediately tested. Lawrence is capable of wrecking any game plan the Ravens have if they can’t block him. The offensive tackles will also need to be up to the task against Boye Mafe, Myles Murphy and Cedric Johnson on the edge.

The Ravens will be similarly tested on defense in the secondary, where they’re tasked with slowing down Cincinnati’s high-powered passing attack. Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins have given the Ravens issues over the years, and they will need a strong performance from Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey on the outside to limit explosive passing plays. Getting consistent quarterback pressure, like the Ravens did last week in Cleveland, will be important to make Joe Burrow uncomfortable.

Cincinnati Bengals

Matchup: @ Baltimore Ravens, 1:00pm EST

On the other side of this week’s AFC North showdown, the Bengals are fresh off a bye week and heading into Baltimore with extra rest and preparation time. Before their break, they snapped a two-game losing streak with a 31-24 win over the Miami Dolphins to get back over .500 by one game. Both Chase and Higgins were playing off of injuries in that game, so the bye week came at a good time for the Bengals to get extra healthy.

If Jackson is not playing, the defensive task becomes much easier for the Bengals. Like the Browns did last week, the Bengals will likely crowd the box at the line of scrimmage and play tight man coverage — forcing Huntley to beat them downfield. The Ravens have not been as efficient running the ball this season and have struggled in short-yardage conversion attempts with Derrick Henry. If the Bengals can control the line of scrimmage with their defensive front, they should be able to find some defensive success regardless of the quarterback.

The Ravens’ defense has played a lot of two-high safety looks and dared offenses to beat them in the middle of the field. The Bengals will likely try to establish the run in a difficult road environment, but that’s been an area of weakness for them this year. Their 82.8 rushing yards per game ranks fifth-worst in the NFL, while they’re in the Top 10 in passing yards. In 10 career games against the Ravens, Chase has totaled 75 receptions and 1,204 receiving yards with eight touchdowns.

Cleveland Browns

Matchup:@ Tennessee Titans, 1:00pm EST

The Browns continue to defy expectations and improved to 4-2 with a win over the Ravens last week, reclaiming first-place position in the division. Like their previous three victories before, the Browns won by four points or less and their win came via a late fourth quarter scoring drive to take the lead. Whether or not this is sustainable remains to be seen, but they’ve put themselves in good position thus far regardless.

A more favorable contest is on the docket this week against a one-win Titans team, who the Browns are narrow favorites to beat on the road. It’s projected to be another low-scoring affair. The Browns’ defense should be able to handle Tennessee’s offense with relative ease. The Titans are averaging just 14.0 points per game, tied for the worst mark in the league, and have the least productive passing attack of any team. They are coming off a season-best showing, however, having scored 26 points in their first win of the season last week.

The Titans’ defense has been much more formidable, led by star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons up front, who is a game-wrecking talent. The Browns have continued to struggle running the ball, but Tennessee is vulnerable against the run, allowing over 122 rushing yards per game. Getting Quinshon Judkins back from injury would be a nice boost for this game. He’s on track to play after returning to practice this week in limited fashion.

item.title: Our Defense vs. Their Offense: Pittsburgh Steelers
item.description: Saints defense needs to get right against a manageable Steelers offense
item.content:encoded:
This game between the Steelers and the Saints will be determined when the Saints’ defense is on the field. The Steelers’ offense will feature Aaron Rodgers in his second season as their quarterback, and his primary target will be DK Metcalf. Metcalf is a physical freak and a matchup nightmare because of his combination of size and speed.

However, the Steelers have not been explosive offensively so far this season. They are averaging only 320 yards per game, with 221 passing yards and 99 rushing yards per game. Jaylen Warren is a very physical running back who is difficult to take down. The Saints will have to make sure they are ready to hit and wrap him up. He will run through arm tackles and rarely go down on first contact.

The Steelers are also averaging 22.8 points per game, so this offense is very steady as it goes.

The biggest issue the Steelers have on offense is their inability to protect the quarterback. So far, they have surrendered 19 sacks in six games. This is where Chase Young, who is currently tied for third in the NFL with 5.5 sacks, should get very excited.

The issue here, though, is the matchup. As average as the Steelers’ offense is, the Saints’ defense has just been bad. The Steelers rank 20th in rushing yards and 18th in passing yards per game. Defensively, the Saints rank 30th in rushing yards allowed per game, surrendering 138 yards per contest, and 20th in passing yards allowed per game at 239.7.

The Saints’ defense has an opportunity to get right against this opponent. The issues that the Saints have on defense are the same issues the Steelers have on offense, but the same can be said in reverse.

If the Saints’ defense allows the Steelers’ offense to find a rhythm by establishing a running game and fails to put Rodgers into obvious passing situations, this game could get out of hand.

The Steelers’ defense is already a challenge in itself for the Saints’ offense, but the Saints do not want Pittsburgh to play complementary football in Paris.

If anything, this defense should come out aggressively, look to get in Aaron Rodgers’ face, and hit him early and often. This is a great opportunity for defensive coordinator Brandon Staley to turn this defense around.

item.title: Vikings vs. Colts: Can Minnesota Avoid the Ultimate Trap Game?
item.description: 5-0 Vikings must prevent a trap game vs the Colts to stay perfect.
item.content:encoded:
The 5-0 Minnesota Vikings face a motivated Indianapolis Colts team coming off their bye week—and every sign points to a classic NFL trap game. In this episode of The Real Forno Show, host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano break down why Sunday’s matchup against the Indianapolis Colts has all the makings of a trap game—and why Minnesota must avoid complacency at all costs. Coming off a bye week with 97 of 98 analysts picking them to win, the Vikings face a Colts team that just fired general manager Chris Ballard. “This screams trap game,” Forness said. Stefano outlined the anatomy of a trap game: “A trap game is not merely a game against an inferior opponent. It’s a confluence of a record disparity, motivational symmetry, scheduling context, and cognitive load.”

Forness emphasized that ball control may be the Vikings’ ticket to a Super Bowl run. “This offense’s number one job isn’t necessarily to score points, it’s to keep the defense off the field,” he explained. The Vikings have held the ball for over 79 minutes in their last two games, limiting Brian Flores’ top-ranked defense to just 84 snaps. Forness compared the approach to college football: “Ball control and time of possession. It’s ugly… But God, there’s beauty in watching Army versus Navy.”

On the defensive side, Flores’ unit ranks first in the NFL in points allowed at 12.8 per game and presents a nightmare for Colts quarterback Daniel Jones, who has 15 turnover-worthy plays this season. “Eric Wilson should not be this good at football, but it’s a tribute to what Brian Flores is doing,” Forness said of the 10th-year journeyman linebacker turned Pro Bowl candidate. The Colts also feature the league’s worst run defense by EPA per rush allowed, setting up Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason for a potentially big day on the ground.

Key Points:

  • The Vikings have historically struggled coming out of the bye under Kevin O’Connell, losing to the Eagles in 2024 and the Lions in 2023.
  • The Colts fired GM Chris Ballard mid-season, adding emotional motivation; Anthony Richardson publicly praised Ballard despite being benched.
  • Indianapolis ranks last in the NFL in pressure percentage and EPA per rush allowed.
  • Kyler Murray has just 18 available snaps with Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and T.J. Hockenson all on the field together.
  • The Colts’ offensive line features Jalen Travis starting over Bernhard Raimann at left tackle, with Tanor Bortolini vulnerable against cross-dog blitzes.
  • Brian Flores’ simulated pressures and six-plus-man blitzes will test Daniel Jones, who remains less than a year removed from a torn Achilles.
  • Forness predicted a 27-16 Vikings victory, calling it “ugly” but effective: “It’s okay to win ugly.”
  • The Colts’ star tight end Tyler Warren and wide receiver Alec Pierce are trending toward not playing.
  • Shane Steichen’s tendency to abandon the run—even when leading—could play into Flores’ hands.
  • “As long as you win, baby,” Forness said. “All that matters is you win another game.”

item.title: The Ravens are in a playoff spot again without even playing a game
item.description: The Baltimore Ravens have moved into playoff position without even playing a game.
item.content:encoded:
The Baltimore Ravens didn’t even play a game but moved from OUT to IN in the AFC playoff race. The New England Patriots lost on Thursday night to fall to 4-3, meaning all the 4-2 teams moved up including the formerly eighth-place Ravens. Baltimore now occupies the seventh and final playoff spot in the AFC.

AFC playoff standings following the Patriots’ loss

1. Kansas City Chiefs (5-0)

2. Buffalo Bills (5-1)

3. Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2, win over CLE)

4. Cleveland Browns (4-2, 2-0 vs PIT & BAL, loss to JAX)

item.title: The Return of Kenneth Walker
item.description: Hear me out. Could the Seahawks just lock up the visiting locker room after Sunday night’s game and not let Kenneth Walker III leave the building? It’s always bittersweet when a former star comes back to town for the first…
item.content:encoded: Hear me out. Could the Seahawks just lock up the visiting locker room after Sunday night’s game and not let Kenneth Walker III leave the building? It’s always bittersweet when a former star comes back to town for the first time, and Walker, Super Bowl MVP just eight months ago, should get a standing ovation when he steps into Lumen Field Sunday night for the Chiefs-Seahawks game. But it’s been made all the more bittersweet by the failure of Seattle’s plan to replace him, at least through six weeks. Zach Charbonnet was activated from the PUP list Thursday, and intends to play this weekend, which will help. But he’s probably still a ways away from being at full strength, so counting on him to single-handedly boost the Seattle run game is probably a bit much. First-round pick Jadarian Price, meanwhile, remains on injured reserve with his chest injury, and won’t be eligible to return for a couple more weeks. And so, at least for a little while, the 30th-ranked run offense in DVOA will have to continue to try to make ends meet with the likes of Emanuel Wilson and George Holani playing major roles. This has been a problem and will continue to be a problem; it’s just extra highlighted when the guy you could have kept is standing on the other side of the field. The Seahawks could, conceivably, have franchise-tagged Walker instead of re-signing Rashid Shaheed. John Schneider and company do not like paying significant money to a running back, and it’s true that you can find acceptable running back play for much less than the $14.4 million a year he’s getting to be the missing piece in the Kansas City offense. It’s just that you do actually need to find acceptable running back play. Maybe Charbonnet will be that when he returns, but until now, Seattle’s running backs have been almost comically below replacement level. It’s almost unsporting to compare Walker’s stats to what the Seahawks have done since he left. Stats iQ lets you do that anyway. There’s obviously a little bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison going on here, as Walker gets to run behind the Kansas City line, while the other three have to run behind Seattle’s comparatively motley crew. Kansas City’s offensive line is fifth with 4.76 adjusted line yards, while the Seahawks’ 3.96 ranks 18th, firmly in the middle of the pack. Add in a more functioning passing game at the moment, and Walker gets the benefit of around three quarters of a yard more per carry before anyone touches him then any Seahawks rusher. That’s not likely to change dramatically when both Charbonnet and Price are healthy. The return of Anthony Bradford will give the line a boost and may open up more lanes, making things a little bit better for everyone, but the offensive line really isn’t the major problem here. Ranking 18th in adjusted line yards shouldn’t produce the 30th-ranked team in DVOA. Other metrics, like ESPN’s run block win rate, have Seattle lower, but even they’re they are “only” ranked 25th. Ball security has been a major problem, as the Seahawks have put the ball on the ground six times on rushing plays already this year. Remove fumbles from all teams, and Seattle’s run DVOA would rank 23rd at -11.2%. That’s still bad, mind you, just better than the very bad results they’ve gotten from putting the ball on the ground once a game. Taking out the turnovers kind of matches Seattle’s performance to ESPN’s view of their line, and some of those fumbles are at least aided by offensive line failures, such as George Holani’s fumble on the goal line against San Francisco. But you can’t blame all of Seattle’s struggles on the offensive line, or on turnovers. Maybe the lack of push up front explains why Seattle is dead last in power success and only 26th avoiding getting stuffed. But even when they get past the line, Seattle ranks just 20th in second-level yards and 25th in open-field yards. The thing to remember about Seattle’s run attack last year was that it wasn’t consistently good, and that’s not what Seattle needs to get things going once again. Seattle was 14th in rushing DVOA last year at -3.9%, and they were still at -3.6% in the playoffs. Even in the Super Bowl, with Walker winning MVP, they really didn’t move the ball all that effectively on a play-by-play basis. Against the Patriots, they had a success rate of just 25.8% and a DVOA of -19.0%. Walker only ranked 35th in success rate last year among qualified backs; they weren’t getting the Kansas City version of Walker last season. It’s easy to see what Walker has done with the Chiefs, setting records for the most rushing yards gained in his first five games and all that. But that’s not what Walker was providing last year in Seattle, and I don’t think it would be what he would be providing this year in Seattle; it’s an entirely different offensive environment. No, what Seattle’s run game was last year was explosive. Walker was third last season with 14.9% of his carries going for 10 or more yards. That’s how he won the Super Bowl MVP award – it was the five 10-plus-yard runs, not all the times he was stuffed at the line. It’s easy to forget that Walker had 16 carries of two yards or less in the Super Bowl – and, indeed, six that failed to gain a single positive yard. The highlights burned in your brain are of Walker bouncing to the outside and gashing New England for huge gains – a Timmy Smith or Marcus Allen sort of performance, rather than just grinding things out. That was Walker’s job all year long, and Seattle leaned on those sorts of runs more than most teams. Every team gets worse if you remove their explosive runs from the data – turns out, runs for 10 or more yards are pretty good. But the 2025 Seahawks had the seventh-largest drop last year, falling a full 24.8%, and dropping from 14th to 21st in rushing DVOA. The Seahawks also had the fifth-lowest success rate when you take out their explosive runs, at just 35% – 28th in the league. But that didn’t matter so much, because Seattle’s offense was all about explosive plays over down-to-down consistency, whether that was bombs to Jaxon Smith-Njigba or Walker dashing around the outside. Their offense was like Cal Raleigh’s near-MVP season for the Mariners that season – far too many strikeouts, but you live with that when you’re blasting 60 home runs. The 2025 Seahawks were the Three True Outcomes offense. Well, Raleigh came crashing back to earth last season and so has the Seahawks’ offense. They are not nearly consistent enough on a down-by-down basis to live with just an 8.8% explosive run rate. 8.8% isn’t even all that bad, ranking 17th so far this season, but when your offensive success is predicated on hitting those home runs, you can’t survive that sort of dramatic drop. When Seattle hasn’t managed an explosive run this season, their success rate is 32%; a little lower than 2025, but not dramatically so. They could live with the plays where Wilson or Holani are slamming into the line and getting nowhere if they would find a hole and make some magic happen more than once every dozen attempts. They did just fine last year doing exactly that. This is a team built to punch you in the mouth with defense over and over and get just enough huge gains on offense to put you away. Last season, the average Seahawks touchdown drive lasted just 6.3 plays, the lowest in the league by a substantial margin. This year again, their average touchdown drive is only 6.5 plays long. Seattle doesn’t really score unless they get a big play – and with those big plays drying up on the ground, so has Seattle’s touchdown rate. Last year, Walker was carrying the running game doing just that. Without it, you get lots of thinkpieces talking about just what Seattle is doing wrong. Hey, it’s a living. The Chiefs, it should be noted, were in the opposite situation last year. They had a better success rate with their running game, very rarely getting stuffed at the line. But they had the second-lowest explosive run rate in the league. They had the smallest drop in DVOA when taking out runs of 10-plus yards, because they just didn’t have that many 10-plus yards to take out to begin with. Kareem Hunt and Isiah Pacheco more or less got what they were blocked. Hunt, in particular, was fifth in success rate but fourth worst in explosive rate among qualified running backs. Walker’s success rate has jumped going to Kansas City because he’s also very capable of picking up the yards blocked for him; his success rate of 48.1% is essentially identical to Hunt’s 47.9% last year. That’s kind of where running backs don’t matter – the Chiefs could throw a lot of guys behind their line who could pick up three yards a pop behind their blocking. But Walker then gets those yards, and keeps going, avoiding more tackles than anyone else in the league and turning an OK play into a great one. He led the league in avoided tackle percentage last year, and he’s doing it again in 2026 (Stats iQ link). So, what’s the answer for Seattle? It’s not going to be Charbonnet, one of the least explosive rushers in the league last year. Charbonnet will be better than George Holani, but a bag of footballs given a slight push might be better than Holani at this point. But for those vital explosive plays? They kind of need to count on Price. Price was the less explosive of the two Notre Dame backs in the draft, but Jeremiyah Love was never going to fall to pick 32. And Price does have mondo speed and can turn on the jets when he gets into open space. We’ve seen a little of that so far. His 17.9% explosive rate? Identical to Walker’s, and the third highest in the league…so long as you drop the qualifying threshold to just 25 carries. Price is worse than Walker in basically every other stat so far, but then, so is basically every other running back this season. We have seen, on a handful of carries, Seattle’s vision. They have gambled a big chunk of what made their offense work last year on a younger, cheaper, unproven player. That gamble hasn’t failed yet, but you’ll have to forgive Seattle fans a little bit of seller’s remorse when Walker shows back up Sunday night.

item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts head to US Bank Stadium to face the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. The Vikings are looking healthy coming off a bye and will be excited to continue their undefeated start. The Colts are coming in a little more beat up and they’re having a rough start to the season.

Series Record: 9-18-1

Home Record: 9-6-1

Streak: W2

Largest Win: Vikings 52 – Baltimore Colts 14, September 28, 1969

Largest Defeat: Colts 34 – Vikings 6, December 18, 2016 (Adrian Peterson’s last game playing for the Vikings)

  • We always take a moment to enjoy the largest comeback in NFL History that occurred on December 17, 2022. The Vikings came back from a 33-0 deficit against the Matt Ryan led Colts.
  • The Vikings’ 1st ever playoff game came against the Baltimore Colts Decmeber 22, 1968, a 24-14 Colts win.
  • The following year Joe Kapp went off for a NFL tying record 7 TDs in a 52-14 Vikings victory.
  • Andrew Luck’s 1st win was against the Minnesota Vikings in 2012.
  • Daniel Jones has a 0.67 TD to INT ratio for the season.
  • Jonathan Taylor is averaging a career low 4.0 YPC and has yet to record a 100 yard game this season.

This is a game the Minnesota Vikings should win. The Colts are giving up a staggering 27.3 points per game vs the Vikings stingy 12.8. Daniel Jones has struggled to find the rythym he had last season. The Colts defense is one of the worst in the league with inexperience throughout the lineup. I can’t see the trends changing, but you never know with the NFL.

Minnesota Vikings 20 – Indianapolis Colts 6

item.title: Raiders news: Andrew Janocko sees Michael Mayer as valuable piece
item.description: Las Vegas Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko sees the value in their tight Michael Mayer.
item.content:encoded:
The Las Vegas Raiders are preparing for their matchup with the Los Angeles Rams. It will be their chance to end a three-game losing streak after starting 3-0.

Michael Mayer will look to duplicate his Week 6 performance. He had a career game last week for the Silver and Black. 95 receiving yards was his highest total since being drafted into the NFL. He has become a vital piece in the passing game.

The Raiders coaching staff is not surprised. Offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko spoke of his value to the team during his press conference on Thursday.

“Yeah, Mike [Mayer] is a valuable piece to this team because of the person that Mike is,
starting with that. So, you start with an ultimate competitor. You start with somebody that comes to work
each and every single day, and then you take the football skill set and how he has developed as a player,
how he’s developing in a leadership role. He’s going to be a part of our success going forward.”

His stats this season were expected. Janocko loves his work and study habits as Mayer is in the front row during team meetings.

“I think you just watch Mike [Mayer work every single day in everything he does, run
game, pass game protections, and how he takes nothing lightly. Watching Mike, Mike sits in the front row
of the meeting rooms and just watching him take note and how he pays attention, and then it applies on
the field. It’s just that’s what you look for in a consummate pro.“

Raider Nation should expect Mayer to keep producing in this offense. If teams try to take away Bowers, Mayer’s production will keep rising.

item.title: NFL Playoff Picture: The NFC North just keeps winning
item.description: A look at the NFC playoff picture after the Chicago Bears’ big primetime win on Thursday night.
item.content:encoded:
If you were looking for some pressure off the Detroit Lions on Thursday night, you didn’t get it. The Chicago Bears handled the New England Patriots to move to 5-2 on the season. The win climbs them up to second place in an extremely competitive NFC North, and makes this week’s game between the Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions even more important.

Let’s take a very early look at the NFC playoff picture through six weeks and “Thursday Night Football.”

NFC North standings:

  1. Vikings (5-0)
  2. Bears: (5-2)
  3. Packers: (4-2)
  4. Lions: (3-2)

Chicago is looking like a Super Bowl contender with an offense that is much more under control with Caleb Williams under center, and a very disruptive defense. However, both of their losses have come against divisional foes, which could be a huge tiebreaker factor when it comes to playoff seeding.

Meanwhile, the Vikings will take on the 2-4 Colts Sunday afternoon out of their bye week to try and keep their undefeated season alive. Whoever wins between the Lions and Packers will establish themselves as the third contender in the division.

NFC playoff standings:

Division leaders:

1. San Francisco 49ers (6-0)
2. Minnesota Vikings (5-0)
3. Carolina Panthers (3-2)
4. New York Giants (3-2-1)

Wild Card teams (top three advance):

5. Chicago Bears (5-2)
6. Green Bay Packers (4-2)
7. Detroit Lions (3-2)

8. Seattle Seahawks (3-3)
9. Atlanta Falcons (2-4)
10. New Orleans Saints (2-4)
11. Philadelphia Eagles (2-4)
12. Dallas Cowboys (2-4)
13. Arizona Cardinals (2-4)
14. Los Angeles Rams (2-4)
15. Washington Commanders (1-4-1)

Currently, the Lions hold the final playoff spot in the NFC. The bad news is that the NFC North is extremely competitive and a loss this week would put them in a serious hole in the division.

The good news is the rest of the NFC is not looking very good. Even if Detroit loses this week, they may keep their spot in the final Wild Card position, because the only team that could catch them—the Seattle Seahawks—is playing the Kansas City Chiefs. The Eagles, Cowboys, Rams, and Buccaneers have all been massive disappointments. And while there’s enough time for those teams to turn it around, Detroit has a little wiggle room at the moment to figure out some of their own issues.

item.title: NFL predictions: The Bucs really shouldn’t be a problem for the Panthers
item.description: Panthers vs Bucs is an opportunity for Carolina to prove they are a good team
item.content:encoded:
We’re now at the point of the season where we traditionally would start phasing in heavier coverage of the 2027 NFL Draft and salary cap to provide an optimistic angle towards next season. Unfortunately for our traditions, the Carolina Panthers are actually playing well this year. They are entering the middle of the season as the number three seed in the NFC playoff picture and are forcing their fans to confront the fact that some games should be expected as wins.

I’m not saying that it will be easy. I’m not saying that an off day by Bryce Young or Will Lee III couldn’t derail their entire season’s momentum. But the most-of-Baker Mayfield they’ll be playing against on Sunday, led by the owner of the hottest seat in the NFC South in Todd Bowles, aren’t the kind of team that should be expected to be beat a good team right now. The Carolina Panthers are trying to convince us all that they are a good team. The next step in their argument will always be simple: play the next game on their schedule and play it well.

I think maybe they can do just that. So, too, do the folks over at FanDuel. They’re holding the Panthers as -2.5 point favorites after opening with them as -3 point favorites.

Walker Clement

Panthers 31, Buccaneers 7 -Bryce Young keeps the offense on track, but the wheels start to come off for both Mayfield and Bowles. The reaper may well strike again.

item.title: Giants at Texans matchup: J.J. McCarthy vs. talented Houston defense
item.description: The Giants are starting a new quarterback against the Texans defense. Let’s discuss the matchup.
item.content:encoded:
The 3-2-1 New York Giants travel to Houston to face the 2-4 Houston Texans on Sunday. Houston has won its last two matchups against the Jaguars (34-31) and the Tennessee Titans (26-3). The Texans faced Jacksonville last week in London; Texans’ kicker Ka’imi Fairbairn nailed a 49-yard field goal with zero on the clock to give Demeco Ryans’ team their second win in as many weeks.

The Giants named J.J. McCarthy the starting quarterback for Week 7. McCarthy gives the Giants a mobile quarterback who better fits an offense designed for Jaxson Dart. Still, communication in a loud environment for a young quarterback with less than a month in Giants blue could be an issue for New York. Whatever happens — I’m excited to watch!

Houston’s defense finished second in scoring last year, allowing just 17.4 points per game, and it allowed the fewest yards per game (277.2 yards) while forcing the third-most takeaways (29). The defense isn’t as stout through six games in 2026.

Texans defensive statistics

The Texans rank 20th in points allowed per game (23.8) and 15th in yards allowed per game (329). The Texans rank 27th in passing yards allowed per game (246) while ranking third-best in run defense (83 yards rushing per game). The Texans have 18 sacks through six games, tying for third-most in the NFL.

Houston doesn’t blitz much — the Texans rely on their personnel. They blitz at a 20.7% rate, 29th in the league. Houston is middle of the pack in pressure percentage at 22.7%. The Texans rank 19th in red zone touchdown percentage (62.5%), and the defense ranks 18th in third-down conversion rate (40.78%).

The defense is 14th in EPA per play allowed (–0.02), fourth in defensive success rate allowed (39.8%), with just five total takeaways (23rd in the league). Matt Burke is the coordinator under defensive head coach Demeco Ryans.

Texans’ personnel

The Texans defense aligns in a traditional 4-3. They’re a gap-sound defense with a strong nickel package that has underperformed this season. Star nickel/safety Jalen Pitre missed Week 6 with a sprained AC joint; he’s questionable. Houston’s front seven is among the best in the league.

Edge defender Will Anderson Jr. is a phenomenal player for Demeco Ryans. He has 28 tackles, 7.5 sacks, and 18 pressures. He leads the league in sacks; Danielle Hunter plays opposite Anderson, and Hunter has three sacks with 14 pressures. Jadeveon Clowney and Dominique Robinson rotate into the lineup for Anderson and Hunter.

Sheldon Rankins and Tommy Togiai are the defensive linemen; Rankins has two sacks and five pressures this season. Rookie Kayden McDonald and Logan Hall rotate into the lineup. Linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair is a fast and physical linebacker who has 49 tackles this season. Henry To’oTo’o plays alongside Al-Shaair.

Houston has one of the best secondaries, but it is underperforming and beaten up. Pitre missed last game, and Reed Blankenship — who has struggled this season — was concussed in Week 6. They have two star cornerbacks: Derek Stingley Jr. and Kamari Lassiter, with the latter struggling more in 2026—he’s allowed a 66.7% catch rate on 28 receptions. Stingley, however, has just allowed a 48.5% catch rate.

Callen Bullock and veteran M.J. Stewart could be the starting safeties, with Blankenship dealing with a concussion.

The matchup

The Giants believe McCarthy gives them a better chance against Houston, in part because of his ability to escape and evade from within the pocket. Jameis Winston was sacked 15 times this season, and the offense — which lacks a run game — relied so heavily on Winston’s arm that is historically known for its inconsistency and borderline reckless play.

McCarthy’s mobility will help the Giants’ offense in multiple phases: designed quarterback runs, read plays (zone-read, RPO, etc.), and pocket escapability, while also providing the offense with better overall arm talent. Expect the Giants to lean on read plays when in shotgun, while trying to establish the run with heavier personnel packages. The play-action passing attack will likely have a few bootlegs and move the pocket plays that utilize McCarthy’s ability to operate on the move.

New York should not be shy to take shots when pre-snap coverage is confirmed in one-on-one scenarios to receivers who aren’t Malik Nabers or Isaiah Likely — who will still be the focal points of the offense. McCarthy can let the ball fly, and Malachi Fields and Darnell Mooney have created adequate separation this season, especially the latter of the two.

The Giants should keep up the high motion rate if McCarthy is up to speed on running the offense effectively with pre-snap movement. The Giants should run a similar offense that we saw in Week 1 with Jaxson Dart at quarterback, while calling more plays that get McCarthy moving. Hopefully, McCarthy’s ability to run will lighten boxes for the Giants’ struggling rushing attack, specifically on zone reads.

Zone-read plays with either Tyrone Tracy Jr. or Cam Skattebo should be used by the Giants’ staff. Tracy Jr. can still operate as the third-down back, but a return of involvement for Skattebo, who received zero touches last week, should happen, especially with Najee Harris released. Devin Singletary should also receive his touches.

The health of Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor is crucial, especially against strong power rushers like Hunter and Anderson, who would both be incredibly difficult matchups for Marcus Mbow.

Houston doesn’t need to blitz — and they don’t do it much — but they may look to send the pressure and spy on McCarthy until the young quarterback proves he can defeat the blitz; it will also be a loud environment, so exotic pressure looks could confuse not only McCarthy but the protection with possible young starting tackles.

Final thoughts

The Giants are heavy underdogs heading into Houston with a new starting quarterback. Their offense has struggled to run the football, and McCarthy can hopefully help to spark something for the rushing attack. Still, this is a tough environment, and communication will be key to keeping pre-snap penalties to a minimum, but it could be hard to achieve on the road, given the circumstances. Even if the Giants lose, though, they will have a full week during the bye to assess the situation and improve on their struggles with a new signal caller.

item.title: Five good Texans questions with Big Blue View
item.description: Ed Valentine of Big Blue View joins BRB for five questions
item.content:encoded:
The NFL has its scheduling quirks. Teams face an entire division every year from the opposing conference and by sheer definition you see them every four seasons unless there is some scheduling quirk involved. The New York Giants are one of those teams for the Texans. We don’t have a particular rivalry and we are in opposite conferences, so we will not see them but every four years. By definition, I have done this feature once with Ed Valentine from Big Blue View in the last five seasons doing this feature. The Giants made it interesting by making a quarterback change midweek and that is where our conversation began.

Battle Red Blog: The Giants have tabbed J.J. McCarthy to start this week. What should we expect to see from him? Are Giants fans confident that he can raise the level of play at the position and lead the Giants to the playoffs?

Ed Valentine: I don’t think we really know what to expect. I do know Giants fans think this is the right choice. McCarthy hasn’t been with the team for a month yet, and how comfortable he is with the entire offense is anybody’s guess. He says he can run the entire playbook, but we will see.

He gives the Giants’ offense a jolt of energy, and he brings the quarterback run game back into the offense. The Giants built an offense around Jaxson Dart, and the quarterback run game was a big part of it. That was out the window with Jameis Winston. McCarthy is not the runner Dart is, but he is young, athletic, can run, and puts that part of the playbook back into the arsenal. He also has a big arm, and isn’t afraid to use it.

Can he get the Giants to the playoffs? That’s anybody’s guess. There is probably more upside with McCarthy than with Winston, but he did flop last year in Minnesota and he was No. 3 on the Vikings’ depth chart for a reason.

BRB: Cam Skattebo did not get a lot of carries last week. Has he fallen out of favor following his fumble against Washington?

EV: Cam Skattebo played six snaps and got ZERO carries Sunday against the Saints. He was held accountable for fumbling four times in five games, including three straight. His overtime fumble vs. the Commanders was inexcusable, and cost the Giants a chance to win. The Giants released Najee Harris this week, so Skattebo will most likely be right back in the mix this weekend.

BRB: Malik Nabers is one of the top receivers in the NFL this season. How would you compare him to the other WR1s in the league?

EV: I honestly don’t spend a lot of time studying Justin Jefferson, Ja’Marr Chase, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, etc. That said, Nabers is a tremendous playmaker. He is a top 10 receiver, no doubt.

BRB: Who are some names we haven’t heard of that could make an impact on Sunday?

EV: The Giants don’t really have a bunch of out-of-nowhere guys you probably haven’t heard of. Maybe Trace Ford, a second-year edge defender who was just added to the 53 or kick returner/receiver Charlie Jones, who caught his first two passes with the Giants last week.

BRB: The Texans opened as heavy favorites (7.5 advanced to 10 points) according to Fanduel. How do you see the game going? Are there any prop bets you feel comfortable recommending?

EV: I think this is a difficult game for the Giants. I fear that the Texans defense, which has not been right this season, will have a get-right game. Prop bets are not my thing. I don’t pay much attention.

item.title: Why the Falcons need to prioritize Kyle Pitts to solve passing game woes
item.description: It’s another season where a coaching staff has to figure out how to consistently utilize the dynamic pass-catcher.
item.content:encoded:
With less than 11 minutes left in the fourth quarter, Kyle Pitts caught his second pass on a quick out as the Falcons trailed 31-7. It’s normally a standard route and play for a tight end to make in a lopsided matchup. It became the spark the Falcons needed for an unexpected comeback attempt. It also could prove to be the platform to help combat one of the most pressing issues surrounding the Falcons.

The Bears soundly outplayed them in every phase of the game, making it an uncompetitive matchup at one point in the second half. The defensive front got bulldozed out of gaps and struggled to maintain its rush integrity against Caleb Williams. The special teams were an absolute disaster, headlined by Zachariah Branch’s nightmare performance that every rookie dreads.

Despite those glaring shortcomings and breakdowns, the most damaging aspect of the loss was how overwhelmed the offense looked against Chicago’s pressure looks.

For the second consecutive game, Michael Penix Jr. looked incapable of making the right reads and throwing accurately under pressure for long stretches. The coaching staff’s game plan to combat Dennis Allen’s constant schemed-up pressures should raise plenty of questions.

Penix Jr. still could have operated better with quicker processing and better feel for blindside pressure. It took until the fourth quarter for him to find some rhythm against Chicago’s defense when they rushed five or six.

That’s when Penix Jr. connected with Jahan Dotson for 32 yards on a stop route, where Dotson made a nice hesitation move that turned a solid completion into an explosive gain. It was a sharp play beating Chicago’s five-man pressure.

Dotson’s career inconsistency and overall limitations make you cautious about his ability to create separation on the outside often enough to give Penix Jr. high-percentage looks against blitzes. What Pitts did on the next play can be replicated, albeit hopefully not as dramatically for the sake of the Falcons.

Dangerous in the slot

Per Pro Football Focus, Pitts ran 17 routes from the slot versus Chicago. That was a season high, easily surpassing the seven he ran against Carolina. Some of the high usage from the slot can be attributed to the game script. It was the first game this season where the Falcons were behind all game long with Penix Jr. under center. That proved to be a recipe for success after three quarters of a mostly inept dropback passing game.

Chicago brought six with former Falcon Clark Phillips rushing in unblocked. Penix Jr. had to get the ball out quickly again to Pitts outside the numbers. The throw was inside of Pitts, allowing Elijah Hicks to close in for a potential interception. Somehow, the 2025 second-team All-Pro tight end ripped the ball away and juked past Nick McCloud to produce a remarkable 29-yard gain. In the process, he prevented a certain turnover with his improved contested-catch ability.

Those types of completions could be an instant solution to the Falcons’ problems against crowded fronts and blitzes. Whether defenses only rush four or bring the entire house with seven or somewhere in between, Baltimore and Chicago have provided a blueprint to rattle Penix Jr. by crowding the line of scrimmage with bodies.

Combine that with Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees falling short of answers schematically, and you get a dropback passing game that severely limits the offense. That can’t happen against top-tier teams like the Ravens and Bears.

Three plays after the highlight-reel reception, Pitts was in the slot again on third down. Chicago rushed six, with Allen being relentless in trying to force Penix Jr. into another off-target throw or sack. Instead, the young quarterback found Pitts uncovered, as Hicks couldn’t make up the ground to stop him. It was a routine touchdown, but it showed how Pitts can be a dependable solution to a glaring problem.

Despite being such a unique talent as a deep threat, Pitts can be maximized in the short-to-intermediate areas of the field. He proved last year that he can consistently make defenders miss and run through contact after the catch. His blocking has improved enough that he can play more in-line and create more mismatches with his explosiveness off the line of scrimmage.

While he should be used more in the slot following Olamide Zaccheaus’ poor play and Branch’s disastrous game, Pitts can also line up more traditionally as a tight end to bolster the Falcons’ aerial attack.

Being quick and decisive

After Jessie Bates connected on his signature peanut punch to force a fumble, as he does multiple times a year, it didn’t take long for Penix Jr. to go back to Pitts. Operating in no-huddle, they slowed Chicago’s pressure plan and capitalized on Pitts being isolated inside with an undersized defensive back. 

Targeting that mismatch helped Penix Jr. find Pitts to convert on third and nine. They connected again on the next play to get in the end zone, putting the Falcons within striking distance of an outrageous comeback. A slight rub by Zaccheaus on the slant-flat concept gave Pitts the space necessary to score his second touchdown of the game.  

As much as fans want to see Pitts be utilized like the unicorn he was projected to be, the coaching staff needs him more than ever as a possession pass-catcher in these situations to give Penix Jr. an immediate option under pressure.

There will be instances where he can thrive in the slot, like against Chicago. He could also line up as an in-line tight end, chipping an edge rusher and serving as a reliable outlet underneath. Whatever the play design, Pitts needs to be a bigger focal point to make the passing game more efficient. 

According to TruMedia, the Bears blitzed Penix Jr. on an alarming 48.7 percent of his dropbacks. That could increase in upcoming matchups against Todd Bowles, Steve Spagnuolo, and Brian Flores. Those coaches won’t hesitate to ramp up the pressure on any quarterback, let alone a young passer who isn’t reacting well when seven defenders are lined up across the line of scrimmage. 

The coaching staff will have to do its share schematically to solidify their protection plan. Making Pitts a bigger focal point in the passing game is the other vital step to punish defenses for constantly blitzing. Signs are emerging in recent weeks, as Pitts’ target share has increased over the last three games.

That said, those targets have to come earlier in games. Pitts catching only his second pass late in what was arguably the Falcons’ most disappointing performance of the season (with a starting-caliber quarterback under center) indicates he needs to be prioritized far more early and often.

item.title: Is A.J. Brown growing frustrated by his lack of production? Patriots star says ‘No.’
item.description: The wide receiver has caught just three of 16 targets since his return to the Patriots offense.
item.content:encoded:
After every New England Patriots game, we are publishing an admittedly subjective list of “winners and losers.” A.J. Brown found himself included in each of the last two editions, and both times in the “loser” category.

Why? Because the big-ticket offseason acquisition failed to live up to expectation against the New York Jets in Week 6 and again versus the Chicago Bears on Thursday night. In total, he has caught just six passes on 16 targets in those two games, gaining 75 yards in the process.

His lack of production as the Patriots’ No. 1 wide receiver has been notable. Brown himself is not stressed or frustrated by it, however.

“I’m a vet, I understand how the game goes,” he explained after the Patriots’ 30-24 loss in Chicago. “It’s just how the game is. I know what type of player I am and I know that that’s always the case, every time I line up I get a lot of attention. Teams try to take me away and it gives a lot of opportunities to other guys to make plays and soften that up for me. And then whenever I get my shots, I have to make them.”

So far, Brown has not been able to make the shots on a regular basis. Against the Bears, he had a deep ball broken up at the catch point — a play that could have been flagged for defensive pass interference — and saw two other targets fall incomplete.

He did catch passes of 18, 16 and 14 yards for his best output as a Patriot to date, but the team did not send two draft picks to the Philadelphia Eagles earlier this year for 48 yards’ worth of production. He was brought in to help lift Drake Maye and the passing offense to new heights, and so far has not delivered on that promise.

Of course, the circumstances played a role in this as well. In the season opener in Seattle, Brown caught three passes in just over two quarters of play before exiting with a high ankle sprain. He missed the subsequent four games on injured reserve, and has participated in only four non-walkthrough practices since his return last week.

The 29-year-old knows that he cannot force the issue, and neither can his quarterback.

“Drake did a really good job just taking what they gave us. You can’t force that,” he said. “It’s tough, but you can’t get aggressive. You can’t get emotional and try to force something. I think he did a great job just taking what they gave us, and unfortunately in the first half we were just stubbing our own toe.”

item.title: The Cowboys offense hasn’t been this flat in a while
item.description: The Cowboys offense hasn’t been this flat in a long time
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys have a lot of problems right now. Speaking in a macro sense, they exist on both sides of the ball. The defense has been moribund for a long time now so struggles there are hardly new. We unfortunately know to expect the team to have issues there.

But entering this season it was a foregone conclusion, well beyond an assumption, that the offense would at least take care of business and therefore give the team a chance. They started off this season in a manner that wasn’t quite “GOTI” level, but they at least looked like a group that could somewhat live up to that idea.

That has not been the case over the last two weeks.

We haven’t seen the offense this low in a long time

Combing through the insights from NFL Pro for this week’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles unveiled something that really surprised me, and it really captures how and why it feels like the offense is broken in a way that it hasn’t been in a long time.

Consider that the Cowboys have only scored 29 points over their two-game losing streak. Before we go further, let’s stipulate that going off of ‘points scored’ is casting a very, very, very vague net over things, but this tidbit is still interesting.

The 29 points that the Cowboys have scored in this two-game span are the fewest that they have scored in any two-game span where Dak Prescott started and finished both games in question since Weeks 12 and 13 of the 2019 season.

Dallas barely squeaked out 24 points against the New England Patriots and Buffalo Bills (Thanksgiving) during that span, and a few weeks later Jason Garrett would not be asked to return as the team’s head coach. It is also worth adding context that this was the first year in which Kellen Moore was the team’s offensive coordinator.

But holy cow. Obviously the qualifier of Dak starting and finishing both games in question moves the goalposts of spans a little bit, but that is necessary to fully evaluate what is happening here. Consider that the 2019 span also preceded CeeDee Lamb even being on the Cowboys roster. There is absolutely zero reason for why the offense should be pulling teeth to score right now with Prescott, Lamb, and everyone else healthy and available.

If we are pointing a finger at any one “why” here, it seems that the current book on how to stop the Cowboys is to fluster Prescott specifically with pressure. For so long he was a quarterback who excelled against the blitz, and he has seemingly not been able to thrive at all against them in these last two games.

NFL Pro also noted that Prescott has thrown over 60% of his passes short (so within 0-9 air yards) over the span in question. It was 61.9% against the Buccaneers and 63% against the Packers, if you are curious.

Dak has had a short pass rate of at least 60% a total of five times throughout the Brian Schottenheimer era and all five of those have been losses. If you can get to him quickly and not allow him time to work downfield with Lamb or George Pickens, your odds are pretty good.

Prescott, Lamb, Pickens, and Schottenheimer all have to find a way to counteract this phenomenon and they have to find a way to do that immediately. If they don’t, they are going to keep running into this challenge and so long as it is effective, why would anybody do anything different?

item.title: Analyst: Rams should trade for Chris Godwin
item.description: Chris Godwin trade rumors and other bits of NFL news on a Friday

Should the Los Angeles Rams make a move for Chris Godwin? The Rams have lost Davante Adams due to injury for an extended period of time and besides Puka Nacua, the receiver room for the Rams is a question mark. Could Godwin help stabilize the room?

Godwin is a veteran of the NFL, he’s won a Super Bowl, but he’s also had some serious injuries that have likely impacted his ability to play at his best. If the Rams could get a prime Godwin, then this trade would be beneficial, but a broken-down Godwin? How much does that help the Rams?

So, L.A. will see in Week 7 if they have enough depth in their wide receiver and tight end group to make up for Adams going down, and if not, then the Rams may want to make a trade. Or if the Rams fall to 2-5, they may want to sell.

If we know one thing about Rams general manager Les Snead, it’s that he loves to wheel and deal. He’s proven throughout his career that he’s not shy when it comes to pulling the trigger on a big trade, so it’s very possible we’ll see the Rams make some sort of deal before the NFL’s Nov. 10 trade deadline gets here.“

item.title: UNC returns to Kenan Stadium to face off against Syracuse
item.description: Here’s what you need to know about Carolina’s next opponent.
item.content:encoded:
Last season, the victory over the Orange marked Bill Belichick’s first win against a Power 4 opponent. This season, a victory will put the Tar Heels on the verge of bowl eligibility. Can North Carolina get the victory against Syracuse for the second straight season?

The Opponent

All-time Record

758–590–49, 17-11-1 in bowl games

Best Former player

Syracuse does have some good former players including Marvin Harrison Sr. (Super Bowl Champion and Hall of Famer), Dwight Freeney (Super Bowl Champion and Hall of Famer), and Art Monk (three-time Super Bowl Champion and Hall of Famer). However, despite all those accolades, the best former player award goes to Jim Brown. Brown was an NFL Champion, a three-time league MVP, a nine-time All-Pro, and a nine-time Pro Bowler. He led the league in rushing yards eight times and in rushing touchdowns five. The NFL Hall of Famer holds four NFL rushing records, including career rushing yards per game and per carry as well as well as the most games with at least four touchdowns. He is twelfth all-time in rushing yards and is considered by many to be the greatest running back of all time (for me it is Barry Sanders, but I would not argue with you about Brown).

Head Coach

Fran Brown. Brown, a former Western Carolina cornerback who also spent time in the NFL with the Cincinnati Bengals, is 15-16 overall in three seasons at the only school he has ever been a head coach. Brown is 6-14 in ACC play and 1-0 in bowl games as the head man in Syracuse. Last season was Brown’s only game against UNC as he will look to even the score and return the home loss he suffered last season.

Last season

Last season, the Orange started off hot going 3-1 with a big road victory over Clemson. However, starting quarterback Steve Angeli got injured in that game and the wheels quickly fell off the wagon as Syracuse finished the season losing their last eight to finish 3-9 on the season.

When the Tar Heels are on offense

When North Carolina is on offense they should find ways to get the ball to their playmakers: Jordan Shipp, Jelani Thurman, and the running back duo of Demon June and Jaylen McGill. Syracuse is a lower end of the conference defense that is allowing teams to score over 25 points per game, so the offense should be able to take advantage of that as long as Billy Edwards Jr. is getting the ball to the weapons around him.

When the Tar Heels are on defense

When North Carolina is on defense, they need to know where wide receiver Umari Hatcher is at all times. Hatcher leads the ACC with 784 yards, and is tied with Miami wide receiver Malachi Toney for first in the conference with 50 catches while his seven receiving touchdowns is second behind Toney’s eight. If UNC loses track of Hatcher like they did with Notre Dame’s Jordan Faison, it will be a long day for the defense. Additionally, the Tar Heels should keep an eye on running back Tylik Hill, who is tenth in the ACC in rushing yards and could cause problems for this defense if not properly contained.

This game was always one of the “winnable” ones on the Tar Heels’ schedule. With their recent surge, it becomes even more important with North Carolina getting closer to bowl eligibility in Bill Belichick’s second season. Additionally, for probably the first time this season, UNC should have the better quarterback of the two and should be able to control the game and get the victory.

What do you think about the Tar Heels’ next opponent? Let us know in the comments below.
