RP: The first thing you’ll notice about the Saints offense is that while they have a dismal rushing attack and middling overall passing numbers, they also are somehow a top-10 scoring offense. Don’t be too alarmed, though. While there are some talented playmakers, and Kellen Moore is an offensive mind I view favorably, a slightly deeper examination of the Saints reveals they are more of a paper tiger.

For starters, the Saints have not faced many difficult defenses at this point in the season. Consider the points allowed per game rankings of five of their six opponents:

  • Detroit (29.6 / 30th)
  • Las Vegas (27.0 /26th)
  • Atlanta (25.5 / 23rd)
  • New York Giants (23.3 / 19th)
  • Baltimore (22.0 / 15th)

Not exactly a murderers’ row of defenses. When the Saints did face a strong defense — the Vikings, who allow the fewest points per game (12.8) — they predictably folded, losing 23-13. I suppose some props should be awarded for clearing the Vikings’ season average.

Also consider that the Saints offense has often been late to the party. New Orleans is averaging just 7.2 points in the first half of games this season. All told, they have run 215 plays while trailing against just 26 plays while holding a lead.

A big factor in this is their ineffective running game. Some of this is due to losing starting tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. early in the season, which has forced 2023 fifth-round pick Asim Richards into a starting role. Richards has the 10th-worst run-blocking grade from Pro Football Focus among tackles with at least 100 run-blocking snaps this season. Some of the Saints’ struggles are also due to losing prized free agent signing Travis Ettiene Jr. to injury in Week 3, though he had struggled prior to injury, failing to top 57 yards in a game. In his absence, that has left a rotating trio of Kendre Miller, a past-his-prime Alvin Kamar, and CJ Donaldson. None of them have found consistent success.

The Steelers should be prepared to see a lot of inside zone against the Saints. So far this season, they’ve called 88 zone running plays compared to 31 gap runs, and their rate of inside run calls (64.3%) is second highest in the league. Regardless of what they call, the underlying metrics spell out how ineffective they’ve been. New Orleans averages just 3.8 yards per carry (T-19th), with an average of just 0.97 yards before contact (21st), and 2.84 average yards after contact (16th). They’ve been stuffed at the 14th-highest rate (16.9%), have a 39.6% success rate (T-17th) when running, and are failing to create explosive runs with just 12 runs of 10-or-more yards (T-20th). They are also averaging a half-yard less rushing yards than expected per rush, the fourth-worst mark in the league.

Because the Saints struggle to run the ball and are always trailing, a lot of strain is then put on the shoulders of second-year quarterback Tyler Shough. A former second-round pick who had a longer-than-usual college career due to injuries, Shough is in many ways a cool story for the Saints. Right now, he’s tied for the second-most passing touchdowns in the NFL. In fact, he has the same number of touchdowns (12) and interceptions (5) as Aaron Rodgers this year. Shough also has the 10th-lowest sack rate (5.2%), and he’s been making quick decisions with the eighth-quickest average time to throw (2.73 seconds).

But much like the rest of the Saints’ offense, the underlying metrics paint a more complicated picture for Shough. One reason he might be getting the ball out so quickly is because the Saints give up the seventh-quickest average time until pressure at 2.55 seconds. While they rank 20th in pressure rate (37.6%), the sheer volume of plays New Orleans runs has also allowed them to give up the second-most pressures (97) this year. The Saints don’t run much play-action either, with their 11.9% play-action rate ranked the second-lowest in the NFL.

Like most quarterbacks, Shough’s effectiveness takes a hit under pressure compared to when he’s kept clean. When facing no pressure, Shough completes 72.8% of his passes, racking up 1,012 yards, nine touchdowns, just two picks, and he averages 6.4 yards per attempt at an average depth of target of 6.5 yards. Under pressure, though, Shough’s completion percentage plummets to 49.4% and he’s thrown three interceptions against three touchdowns. His YPA drops to 5.6 while pressured, but oddly enough his ADoT spikes to 12.1, which seems to indicate he throws the ball away or forces attempts downfield when he gets a defender in his face.

So it would seem the simple answer for the Steelers defense is to get pressure on Shough and watch him crack. However, don’t think it will be as easy as dialing up the blitzes. Shough has seen a lot of football for just a second-year player thanks to his prolonged college career. And while his numbers dip when pressure gets home, he has a decent enough head for the game that he’s able to adjust when he knows where the blitz will be coming from. Despite opponents blitzing the Saints at the 10th-highest rate in the league (35.1%), Shough’s completion percentage actually improves when he’s blitzed (66.3%) compared to when he isn’t (64.1%). He’s thrown six touchdowns and three interceptions when blitzed, compared to six touchdowns and two interceptions without a blitz. And with an ADoT of 7.3 yards against the blitz, he isn’t just checking it down to his running back either.

If there’s one secret to stopping Shough beyond getting pressure home, it’s his struggles against zone. Shough’s numbers against man coverage are some of the best in the league, but his efficiency takes a dip when he faces zone.

Perhaps Shough’s struggles with zone coverages might explain why he avoids throwing to the middle intermediate (10+ yards) and deep (20+ yards) parts of the field. Oddly enough, he’s been effective when he attacks the middle intermediate area, going 14-for-15 for 197 yards and two touchdowns, but that’s at an average of less than three attempts a game. And that effectiveness isn’t exactly a fluke, as he went 25-for-31, 383 yards and a touchdown in 10 games in 2025. Again, though, that was at roughly a rate of three attempts per game.

As for the weapons at Shough’s disposal, the one name to circle and highlight is receiver Chris Olave. Through six games, Olave is second in the league in receiving with 580 yards. Olave accounts for 40.2% of the Saints’ total receiving yards and is demanding a 27.1% target rate. The Saints’ passing attack goes as he goes. Olave is a deep threat who is outperforming his career averages on contested catches, converting 62.5% on 16 attempts this season, compared to a 43.4% conversion rate on 92 attempts across his previous four seasons. Olave also doesn’t add much after the catch, averaging 20.8 YAC per game, which ranks 64th in the NFL and 26th among wideouts. Olave has two touchdowns this year and 21 in 61 career games.

Elsewhere, receiver Devoaughn Vele (28 rec, 294 yards, 2 TDs), tight end Juwaun Johnson (25 rec, 248 yards, 3 TDs) and tight end Noah Fant (9 recs, 73 yards, 3 TDs) are other names to keep an eye on, though none of them pose the same threat as Olave. Rookie receiver Bryce Lance is also worth keeping an eye on after he scored his first career touchdown last week.

What to expect from the Saints’ defense

Rushing YPG: 138 (30th)

Passing YPG: 239.7 (25th)

PPG: 29.7 (T-31st)

RB: Tied for the worst scoring defense in the NFL and bottom-10 in a number of other telling metrics, the Saints’ defense has been one of the primary culprits behind New Orleans’ current losing record and third-place ranking in the NFC South.

A surprisingly solid unit in 2025 under coordinator (and former Chargers head coach) Brandon Staley, many expected the Saints defense to take a step forward in 2026. Instead, the group has regressed through six games in 2026, struggling in both the run and pass game. And despite a solid start last week against the Giants, New Orleans gave up a whopping 17 points in the fourth quarter, with New York’s JJ McCarthy entering the game late and tossing for 243 yards.

Starting with that pass defense, the Saints have a young cornerback room led by 2024 draft pick Kool-Aid McKinstry, and 2025 draft picks Jonas Sanker (nickel) and Quincy Riley. At safety, New Orleans has a bit more experience with the duo of Julian Blackmon (two interceptions this year) and Justin Reid. Former Cleveland Browns corner Martin Emerson Jr. has also been a ballhawk for the Saints with a pair of picks last week — expect to see him in the mix more going forward.

However, the Saints are the highest cover-3 team in the league in 2026, and in a mix of allowing too many underneath passes and some poor secondary play, they’ve allowed the sixth-highest completion percentage to opposing quarterbacks this season (66.5%), along with the seventh-highest yards per passing attempt (7.7).

The New Orleans pass rush has seen some success helping out its secondary, with edge Chase Young — once proclaimed as a draft bust — continuing to impress later in his career, currently tied for third in the NFL with 5.5 sacks. His 28 pressures this season are the eighth-most for an edge rusher this season, per Next Gen Stats.

Still, the Saints are seventh-worst in both quarterback pressure rate (31.7%) and time to pressure (2.73 seconds), although a powerful line, led by Young, veteran Cam Jordan, and Carl Granderson (four sacks this season) applied plenty of heat to New York’s quarterbacks last week.

While New Orleans ranks in the middle of the pack in terms of blitz rate (30%), Staley is a heavy user of simulated pressures and loaded defensive fronts in an effort to confuse opposing quarterbacks. That strategy should only get more effective this week with middle linebacker Kaden Elliss moving closer to a return to the lineup.

Elliss, who has recorded 12.5 sacks in the last three seasons, is one of the NFL’s best off-ball blitzers, and could wreak havoc on a Steelers’ offensive line that has struggled with free rushers this season, especially if Aaron Rodgers tries some play-action shots against the New Orleans secondary.

New Orleans could also use Elliss back when it comes to defending the run game, with Pete Werner and second-year linebacker Danny Stutsman having struggled to hold down the fort in the former’s absence. They’ve combined for 10 missed tackles so far this season, with the Saints as a team having the seventh-most in the NFL in 2026.

According to Next Gen Stats, the Saints have missed 16.9% of their tackle attempts on carries by running backs this season, the fourth-highest in the NFL. New Orleans also has the second-lowest stuff rate (12.1%), the sixth-most yards after contact per carry allowed (3.36), the highest success rate allowed on designed runs this season (45.3%), and 0.43 rushing yards over expected per attempt allowed (eighth worst).

This is not a great run defense, and with the Steelers’ Jaylen Warren being especially effective as a play-extending runner (47.5% of his rushing yards have come after forcing a missed tackle this season, the highest among qualified running backs, per Next Gen Stats), Pittsburgh should be looking forward to this matchup.

That’s a lot of stats to say that the New Orleans defensive front, despite having a solid run-stuffer in Davon Godchaux and some up-and-coming talent in Vernon Broughton and Christen Miller, hasn’t been great in containing running backs this year, and the players behind them have struggled to bring them down as well.

A heavy dose of Warren and Rico Dowdle in this game, paired with some of the quick-game concepts the Steelers used against the Buccaneers last week, should be able to move the ball effectively against the Saints in Paris. Pittsburgh is one of the NFL’s best yards-after-catch teams going against the league’s worst tackling defense — that’s a good matchup.

Pittsburgh will also want to use quite a bit of Darnell Washington as an extra blocker against New Orleans’ occasional overloaded fronts. Avoiding turnovers against a struggling secondary that was still very opportunistic last week against the Giants will also be important.

Ultimately, the Saints aren’t one of the more imposing defenses the Steelers will face this year. But New Orleans does come with a lot of young talent that could emerge more this season, and as with all NFL units, they certainly shouldn’t be overlooked.

item.title: 5 things to watch as Jets face Dolphins in Week 7 of 2026 NFL season
item.description: Here are the main storylines as the Jets face the Dolphins in Week 7 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
The Jets came up short in New England, dropping to 2-4 on the season and essentially making this weekend's game another must-win affair. 

They'll be favored at home, with Malik Willis and the winless Miami Dolphins coming to town.

Here are the main storylines to watch as the Jets aim for their first AFC East win under Aaron Glenn…

Miami's best chance for a win?

The Dolphins' season is off to a terrible start after they lost their first five games, and also lost offensive linchpin De'Von Achane to a season-ending injury.

However, they've faced some tough opposition and competed well at times. They should be motivated as they will view this game as their best shot at getting a win.

For the third time in four games, the Jets are facing an opponent that has had longer than seven days to prepare for them, and the Dolphins will no doubt have been doing some soul-searching and specific game-planning during their bye week, which could make them dangerous.

For the Jets, situational football will be under the microscope as they must do better on third and fourth down and in end-of-half situations. New York has been outscored 100-6 in the last two minutes of the first half during Glenn's tenure.

Is D'Angelo Ponds' role set to increase?

The Jets rookie has seen some playing time in recent weeks, and finished the Patriots game in a full-time slot cornerback role after Jarvis Brownlee was apparently benched following some communication breakdowns.

While it's encouraging that the coaching staff's faith in Ponds has increased, he hasn't exactly settled into his role yet, as he had two costly penalties against the Bears and gave up a long catch and a touchdown in New England.

Will Zach Sieler terrorize the Jets once again?

The Dolphins' defensive lineman has developed from being a rotational player into one of Miami's defensive leaders over the past several years, and he always seems to be at his best when facing New York.  

Sieler has played 12 times against the Jets, racking up nine sacks. Miami has a 10-2 record in those games, and he'll be eager to improve on that this Sunday. Otherwise, he could be a trade candidate in the weeks ahead.

Jacob Rodriguez vs. David Bailey

Two of the top contenders for the NFL's Defensive Rookie of the Year award will be facing off.

Bailey is off to a productive start with 31 tackles, five sacks, and three forced fumbles. However, as we've seen in recent weeks, he can be inconsistent and has made mistakes at times.

On the other hand, Rodriguez has been a model of consistency. He has racked up an impressive 57 tackles in five games, with an interception. He's had at least eight tackles in every game apart from the Chiefs game, in which he had three tackles for loss.

Can Omar Cooper Jr. build on his breakout game?

Bailey and his fellow first-round pick Kenyon Sadiq each had a recent breakout game, with Bailey recording three sacks against Cleveland and Sadiq posting a 100-yard game in Detroit. However, neither player has been able to build on that with a big performance since then.

Could Cooper, the Jets' other first-round pick, fare differently in the game after his own breakout? Cooper made his return from IR last Sunday and stepped up with six catches for 103 yards and a touchdown.

It would be nice for the Jets to get more consistency from their rookie class, and that could begin with another good game from Cooper on Sunday.

item.title: Giants DC Dennard Wilson: I wasn't happy with our effort last weekend
item.description: The Giants almost pulled off a stunning comeback after putting quarterback J.J.
item.content:encoded:
The Giants almost pulled off a stunning comeback after putting quarterback J.J. McCarthy in their game against the Saints in the fourth quarter last Sunday, which is a big reason why he'll be starting against the Texans this weekend.

While the offensive coaches prepare McCarthy for his first start as a Giant, defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson is focusing on making sure the team doesn't find itself playing from behind. Next Gen Stats credited the Giants with 18 missed tackles against the Saints and Wilson said at a Thursday press conference that he doesn't believe it was "characteristic" of the team's defense.

Wilson said he specifically "wasn't happy with our effort running to the ball" and explained how he dealt with it this week.

"You confront it. Just like we do, we confront everything," Wilson said, via a transcript from the team. "When you're in the meeting room, you show those plays. I look at guys that don't run to the ball, and I call them traitors because they're traitors to the defense. At the end of the day, when you have a traitor to the defense, you either have to make adjustments to get them off the field, you have to get somebody else on the field, or they have to correct their behaviors. Last week was one of those things where we did not on every play, run to the ball, and it was unacceptable. The guys know it, and this week when you see them out there, they will be flying around 100 miles per hour with their hair on fire."

The Texans have put up 90 points over the last three weeks, so Wilson will need his words to find a willing audience if the Giants are going to avoid a third straight week without a victory.

item.title: Pass rush should determine winner of Packers-Lions
item.description: It might just be as simple as “whoever gets to the quarterback wins.”
item.content:encoded:
When the Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions meet on Sunday afternoon, it will be the first time that the two teams have played since last Thanksgiving. Much has changed since that day, when the Packers won 31-24, but in one sense, nothing has changed at all.

Since that game, Micah Parsons suffered a torn ACL (one that he will not be back from in time for this game) and Zach Bako-Bewele injured his knee (twice) and is out for the season. Edgerrin Cooper also tore his ACL earlier this season. Then there’s the offensive line, where only two players who started for the Packers last Thanksgiving will be in the lineup again in this one, and one of them, Anthony Belton, is playing a different position.

Likewise, the Lions also have just two players from last Thanksgiving’s starting offensive line on the team this week. And of the top 15 players on Detroit’s roster in terms of snaps played on defense in that game, just six are on the roster (seven if Brian Branch is activated off the PUP list by Sunday).

But with all of that under consideration, this game looks like it should still be much the same as the Packers’ other recent games at Ford Field: a track meet with lots of points.

This Sunday, the X-factors for both defenses should be their pass rush. If either unit hopes to slow down the opposition’s offense, it will need to get after the quarterback and, most importantly, get him on the ground. Jared Goff hasn’t thrown a pick yet this season while Jordan Love has been slinging the football like crazy despite heavy pressure. The two are both among the top five quarterbacks in the NFL in passing yards per game as well.

Whichever team is able to get to the opposing quarterback more consistently should win this game, plain and simple. Packers fans will need to hope that defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon can keep confusing yet another offensive line on Sunday to help his players do just that.

Packers winning with element of defensive surprise | Packers.com
Gannon’s creative blitz looks are making it very hard for opposing offensive lines to identify who’s rushing, leading to plenty of pressure on opposing quarterbacks.

Packers’ ball-hawking defense faces unique challenge against pick-free Jared Goff | Packers Wire
Gannon’s goal will be to move Goff off his spot and force him to get the ball out quickly. So far this season, he has not thrown a single interception; will that change on Sunday?

Can Lions get to Jordan Love before Packers receivers get loose? | Packersnews.com ($)
On the other side of the ball, the pass rush is probably the one area where the Lions can actually slow down Green Bay’s offense. If Love has time to throw, he should be able to pick apart a porous secondary, so Aidan Hutchinson and company are Detroit’s best chance to keep the Packers’ passing game in check.

Patriots-Bears on ‘Thursday Night Football’: What We Learned from Chicago’s 30-24 win | NFL.com
Both Caleb Williams and Drake Maye had big games last night, but New England’s run game was MIA while the Bears managed to do enough on the ground late to grind out the win.

Our own Tyler Brooke has reported that the Packers are calling about a quality veteran defensive tackle. It makes sense, too, given the injuries the team has suffered at the position so far.

item.title: 5 things to watch as Giants face Texans in Week 7 of 2026 NFL season
item.description: Here are the main storylines to watch as the Giants face the Texans in Week 7 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
The Giants were in a great position at 3-1 with four seemingly winnable games coming up. 

However, after a tie with the Commanders and a loss to the Saints, they find themselves on the verge of losing their grip on the NFC East if they lose again in Houston on Sunday.

Here are the main storylines to watch as the Giants face the Texans in Week 7…

A tough test against the resurgent Texans

A couple of weeks ago, Giants fans might have been looking ahead to this game as a potentially easy win. The Texans had just dropped to 0-4, losing to a Cowboys team that the Giants beat earlier in the year.

Things have turned around for the Texans since then, though, and they're now hoping for a third straight win that would put them right back in the mix in the AFC South.

Houston blew out the Titans by 23 to get back on track, then outdueled the Jaguars, 34-31, in an exciting shootout in London to improve to 2-4. This is now looking like one of New York's toughest games of the season so far.

J.J. McCarthy makes his first start

The recent trade acquisition has been named the starter for Sunday following a remarkable performance against the Saints last weekend.

McCarthy replaced the ineffective Jameis Winston in the fourth quarter with the Giants trailing the Saints, 34-10. By the end of the game, he had tied the all-time franchise record for passing yards in a quarter and had the Giants on the brink of an incredible comeback.

While the comeback bid ultimately fell short, it was enough to earn McCarthy his shot at starting in Houston. He was 6-4 as a starter last season, and will be eager to get off to a winning start as New York's new QB1.

Can the Giants run the ball on the Texans?

The Texans' resurgence has been credited in large part to head coach DeMeco Ryans taking on a more hands-on role with the defense, but they already had one of the best run defenses in the NFL.

Heading into the London game, they were No. 1 against the run and hadn't allowed any player to rush for 40 yards against them all year. While they actually gave up a season-high 106 yards on Sunday, they have held all of their other opponents to under 90 yards.

New York's own running game appears to be in flux as Cam Skattebo was benched for the second half of Sunday's game after reportedly complaining about a lack of touches, implying that he was being punished for a costly fumble in Washington. Veteran Najee Harris was released after complaining about a lack of touches.

Look for McCarthy to try to contribute to the running game on designed runs and scrambles.

Can Jaylin Noel continue his breakout?

Houston's best known weapon in the passing game is Nico Collins, the two-time Pro Bowler with three 1,000-yard seasons to his name. However, a new star could be emerging.

Previously considered to be mostly a return specialist, the athletic Noel had the biggest game of his career in London as he caught four passes for 107 yards and a touchdown.

Noel showcased where he's been developing his skill set with some impressive route running and good hands in Sunday's game, so he will look for more of the same against New York's banged-up secondary.

Is C.J. Stroud making the leap?

The former second overall pick hasn't had a bad start to his career, but has never really been considered to be playing up to his full potential. While he's posted a winning record as a starter in each of his three seasons, with a 4,000-yard passing season and one Pro Bowl under his belt, Stroud has arguably never looked as good as he does right now.

On course for career-best numbers in virtually every passing category, Stroud posted his third 300-yard game of the season against the Jaguars and has a sparkling quarterback rating of 116.6 over the past three weeks.

He is clearly playing with ultimate confidence right now, as evidenced by some of the tight-window throws he completed in London. It will definitely be a challenge for John Harbaugh's staff to slow Stroud down.

item.title: Could Washington GM Adam Peters try to build around Jayden Daniels at the trade deadline? - Daily Slop
item.description: 2 games behind 1st place Giants and with the league’s 2nd-easiest remaining schedule, could Washington become buyers at the trade deadline?
item.content:encoded:
The Daily Slop – 23 October 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

NFL Trade Deadline

Commanders Roundtable

Should the Washington Commanders be buyers or sellers in 2026?

[E]ven with the argument for the Commanders shifting to a seller with less than three weeks until the trade deadline, there’s also an easy argument as to why the front office should evaluate becoming a buyer.

Quarterback Jayden Daniels’ decision against in-season surgery altered the outlook of the season as a potential season-ending surgery instead became a two-game absence, allowing Washington to avoid a second consecutive lost season due to quarterback injuries. That carries weight because with Daniels on year three of his four year deal ahead of the 2028 team option, the chance for the Commanders’ front office to strike with its franchise quarterback still on its rookie deal carries weight.

Add in the NFC East standings, and Washington still has plenty to play for.

Washington finds itself just two games out from the New York Giants, who sit at 3-2-1 ahead of week seven. Washington also ranks 29th in remaining strength of schedule, per Tankathon, with only Dallas facing an easier slate.

Interior offensive line, secondary and potentially wide receiver with McLaurin sidelined are among the midseason roster needs for the Commanders. Depth along the defensive line has been hit with Javon Kinlaw joining Charles Omenihu and Johnny Newton among the inactives, adding intrigue whether additional reinforcements are needed to upgrade the front seven. The running back room, meanwhile, has lacked star power through six games, even before Jacory Croskey-Merritt was placed on injured reserve.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

The Athletic (paywall)

NFL trade deadline 2026 big board: 50 players who could be dealt before Nov. 10

This is an aggressive list. We wanted to cast as wide a net as possible. Activity around the NFL trade deadline has increased in recent seasons. Last year, for instance, the New York Jets traded away two defensive stars, defensive lineman Quinnen Williams and cornerback Sauce Gardner, for three total first-round picks. Still, most of the players on our board will not be traded. The fun is in considering all the options.

Contracts and the salary cap are important factors in facilitating trades. A team acquiring a player in a trade takes on any unpaid money in that player’s contract. A team trading away a player takes on any already-paid cash as dead money. For each player, we have included a projected 2026 cap hit for the acquiring team. Each figure assumes a trade on deadline day, Nov. 10.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Commanders links

Articles

Commanders.com

NFC East roundup | The division struggled but remains wide open

Giants

Looking ahead to the Houston Texans: The Texans’ No. 3 run defense won’t do the Giants any favors. Houston is coming off a 34-31 victory against the AFC South-leading Jacksonville Jaguars in London. It held Jacksonville’s top rusher, former Commander Chris Rodriguz Jr., to 55 yards on 11 carries.

The Texans announced Tuesday that Tank Dell will return to action for the first time since Dec. 21, 2024, when he suffered multiple torn ligaments and a dislocated kneecap against the Kansas City Chiefs. He’ll likely be on a snap count, but the standout receiver will join a room that also now includes Marvin Harrison, Jr., who had three catches for 34 yards in his debut.

Cowboys & Eagles

The Eagles are riding a four-game losing streak — their longest streak since Doug Peterson’s 4-11-1 season in 2020 and the first in the Nick Sirianni era. Philadelphia will also be without Hurts for the remainder of the season as he recovers from deep blood clots.

The Cowboys have dropped back-to-back games following their 23-13 Sunday Night Football loss to the Green Bay Packers. Both Philadelphia and Dallas enter the matchup with the same 2-4 record, so a victory would push the [the winner] to 3-4 overall [record].

Commanders

What worked: The Commanders almost rallied back from a 23-3 deficit to upset the unbeaten 49ers in the second half. They fell by just one score, 23-17, and the comeback was a valiant effort from Jayden Daniels leading two touchdown drives and a defense that forced three consecutive three-and-outs.

Washington contained San Francisco’s offensive weapons in the second half, namely by bringing Brock Purdy to the ground three times for a total loss of 15 yards and limiting him to just four passes in the final 30 minutes. The defense stepped up in critical moments; Jeremy Reaves recorded an important pass breakup in the secondary that prevented George Kittle from converting on third-and-11, and he also brought Christian McCaffrey down short on a third-and-8.

Although they are tied for No. 1 in the NFL in turnover differential at +6, the Commanders still have a point differential of -40. Washington is generating takeaways and putting pressure on offenses, yet the turnovers aren’t solving its problems on offense and generating points to win games.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Bullock’s Film Room (subscription)

Commanders Film Review: Defense vs 49ers

In the first half, the 49ers offense dominated, scoring touchdowns on three of their first five possessions and were well on their way to another score on the fourth possession before K’Lavon Chaisson punched the ball out and the Commanders got a turnover. In the second half, the 49ers scored a field goal on their first possession and then went three and out on three consecutive drives to end the game.

That makes it sound like the Commanders came out with a terrible game plan and then switched at half time and it all worked perfectly. I don’t think that was the case. But there was a noticeable change in approach early on which didn’t work for Washington at all. That change lines up interestingly with the news that the Commanders have hired Steve Wilks to help with game planning on the defensive side of the ball. Wilks apparently started last week prior to the 49ers game and on the opening drives for the 49ers, we saw a big shift in philosophy from the Commanders defense.

Under Daronte Jones, the Commanders defense are running their interpretation of Brian Flores’ scheme in Minnesota. It’s an ultra aggressive, blitz heavy scheme. But on the 49ers opening possession, the Commanders went away from that philosophy entirely and played a lot more basic zone coverage with just four man rushes up front. It didn’t work for them…

What was new was the continued theme of dropping seven into zone coverage and rushing just four. We’ve seen already this season that the Commanders don’t have the defensive line capable of generating a consistent pass rush with just the front four. So to come into this game with the game plan of rushing four and dropping seven into coverage, rather than persisting with the blitzing style that has been the only form of pressure so far this year, is questionable.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Sports Illustrated

K’Lavon Chaisson is producing for the Commanders

Washington Commanders edge rusher K’Lavon Chaisson did something over the last two games he’s never done before. Chaisson strip-sacked Jameis Winston against the Giants, then eight days later peanut-punched the ball out of Christian McCaffrey’s arms on Monday Night Football. Both plays resulted in takeaways, with Tim Settle recovering the first fumble and Frankie Luvu the second.

item.title: Five Plays: Syracuse Fourth Quarter
item.description: Louisville survived a trip to Syracuse to get a solid road win in the ACC. Below are some of the key plays in the fourth quarter, with some thoughts from me. Louisville turned up the pressure in the second half with blitzes like this one, where Kaleb Beasley comes from the slot. They were able […]
item.content:encoded:
Louisville survived a trip to Syracuse to get a solid road win in the ACC. Below are some of the key plays in the fourth quarter, with some thoughts from me.

Louisville turned up the pressure in the second half with blitzes like this one, where Kaleb Beasley comes from the slot. They were able to confuse the Syracuse offensive line as well as get one-on-one matchups for their best pass rushers. This blitz leads to Ben Perry getting a free run at Malachi Nelson because the left tackle sees Beasley blitzing, but the left guard does not. The guard blocks down, and Perry gets loose.

This was the play where Nelson hurt his shoulder. It’s fair to wonder if this game would have gone differently if he finished this game healthy.

Syracuse ran this play earlier in the game in the same situation, and Ben Perry had to recover to make a nice play to break up the pass. Here, Jabari Mack shows exactly how to play the slot fade on the goal line. He starts the play by angling exactly where he needs to so that he can stay “in phase” with the receiver. Because he’s in phase, there is no path for the ball to get to the receiver unless it goes through him.

Mack then makes a really nice play on the ball by turning and getting his hand on the ball. This is exactly what you want to see from a veteran corner. He stays calm with the ball in the air after using good technique to put himself in position to make the play. Syracuse is forced to kick a field goal, and the Cards keep the lead.

A misconception about man coverage is that you can’t have players with eyes on the quarterback to jump routes or make plays on the ball in the middle of the field. As this play call shows, you can run man-zone concepts with man coverage on the outside and zone on the inside.

Also, as this play shows, your zone players can read the quarterback as Stanquan Clark does here and make a play for the defense. Clark does such a good job of seeing this play develop before he jumps this route. It’s reminiscent of his interception against Ole Miss. This time, he only gets his hands on the ball with Cam White there to pick off the pass.

This may have been the play of the game. Louisville had not had any success on offense in the second half, and the defense had just given them great field position to get some separation on the scoreboard. The drive started off as the others had in the half until Kienholz connected with Jackson Voth on this play.

Lincoln Kienholz did not have a great game, but this was one of the best throws of the season for him. He drives this ball really well right off the top of his drop. The ball placement is absolutely perfect, as it is outside and up where his receiver can make the catch, but the corner would have to make an outstanding play. The corner plays this perfectly, but the throw is perfect, and Voth makes a really good catch before getting up the field for a big play.

I think I point it out every week, but Kienholz’ athleticism is such an asset to this offense. The run game wasn’t working, which means the defense didn’t respect the play action calls like you’d like them to. Kienholz is still able to get outside on this play when a safety has a clean shot at him on the edge. He gets depth while throwing a stiff-arm before he hits Lawayne McCoy on the run.

If this defense could play like this from the first snap, they’d be in much better shape. Jabari Mack closes on this play with a level of effort and energy I haven’t seen from him.

First sack. UofL drops into a cloud zone, and AJ Green and Jerod Smith push the pocket to give Malachi Nelson nowhere to run. Clev Lubin puts on a pass rushing clinic as he gets up the field before retracing his steps into a spin move to get the sack.

Second sack. Tyler Thompson utilizes a similar dip move that he used the week before against SMU. He gets under the arms of the right tackle before diving to get Nelson down as he looks to escape the pocket. All four players did their part to get two straight sacks to essentially close out the game.

What a way to end a game. Stanquan Clark times up the play perfectly and shoots the gap to get a tackle for loss. As frustrating as the first half was, the defense was dominant in the second half. One has to hope that the staff uses the bye week to shift the defense to the more aggressive style of play we saw in the second half.

item.title: Jaguars LT Anton Harrison Reportedly Out For The Year
item.description: Recent reports confirm the worst-case scenario Jaguars LT Anton Harrison. The 2026 season is over for the fourth year OT
item.content:encoded:
Per a recent report from NFL insider Ian Rapoport, Jacksonville Jaguars starting left tackle Anton Harrison will miss the remainder of the 2026 NFL season with a torn ACL. The torn ACL was reportedly revealed during his Thursday surgery.

Harrison was carted off the field at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in the third quarter of the improbable, 19-17 Week 5 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles. He was subsequently placed on IR, with the hope of it just being a three to five week recovery.

Contingency Plan In Motion

While many in the Jacksonville fanbase have been quick to label reserve offensive lineman, Walker Little as an offseason (and in-season) trade piece, the reported news of Harrison’s loss shows exactly why Little has major value on this roster: as a stand-in at both tackle and guard spots. After stepping into the left tackle role for the final quarter against Philadelphia, giving up zero quarterback pressures, Little surrendered just two pressures in Week 6 to the Houston Texans dominant defensive front. The team will need that continued level of play as they continue their playoff push moving forward.

Jaguars Schedule Through November:

  • Week 8: Indianapolis Colts (at home)
  • Week 9: Baltimore Ravens (road)
  • Week 10: Tennessee Titans (road)
  • Week 11: New York Giants (road)
  • Week 12: Tennessee Titans (at home)

With this upcoming slate after the bye week, Jacksonville may be able to weather the early storm, while allowing Walker Little additional time to acclimate next to Emmanuel Pregnon. Notably, the team has Wyatt Milum and Daniel Faalele as additional options to step in as the sixth offensive lineman or new swing guard and tackle.

Impact on Scheme, Negotiations?

Before this injury, Harrison had missed just three games in his first three NFL seasons since being drafted 27th overall out of Oklahoma in 2023. The Jaguars recently picked up his fifth-year option in April, with the accompanying flip from right tackle to left. In terms of his contract negotiations, this injury clearly puts Harrison in an interesting spot also, as he was just settling in on the left side, with a few up and down performances.

While Jacksonville may be one of the better positioned teams to take on the loss of their left tackle, it clearly is a significant loss that will change how they run their offense. For instance, Harrison, in 2025 and 2026 has routinely been left on an island, which allows the Jaguars to play with more receiving options in the field on passing plays. With Walker little sliding in at left tackle, the Jaguars will, presumably, be more prone to providing chips and double teams to both Little and a rebounding Cole Van Lanen at right tackle. This could result in fans seeing more offensive sub-packages, with the team likely leaning into more two tight end sets, 13 personnel, and jumbo packages to slow down the rush. Only time will tell, however.

With Anton Harrison out for the season, how are you feeling about the remaining schedule, Duval? Have the last two games improved your Walker Little reservations? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.

item.content:encoded:
How about cornerback for the Buffalo Bills at the trade deadline?

If so, would Tariq Woolen move the needle? He’s the league’s largest outside cornerback at just over 6’4” and 208 pounds who signed a one-year deal in March with the now 2-4 Eagles. He’s most known for his six-interception rookie campaign, and he’s snagged six since then in the regular season.

This article is the third in the trade-candidate series I plan to sprinkle onto the site until the actual trade deadline until November 10, which is 18 days from now, and lands after Week 9.

Past installments in this series:

Derwin James, Brian Thomas Jr.Jessie Bates

Age: 27

Woolen entered the NFL out of the University of Texas San Antonio in 2022 after one of the craziest combines we’d ever seen at the cornerback position. At his gargantuan size, Woolen ran 4.26 with a 42-inch vertical.

The Seahawks drafted him in the fifth round that year. After the spectacular rookie campaign, Woolen’s ball production cooled, yet he’s established himself as one of the better young physical (and speedy) outside cornerbacks in the NFL.

He was integral on Seattle’s Super Bowl winning defense in 2025, playing 72.8% of the snaps and logging 41 tackles, 12 pass breakups, and a pick during the regular season. In the playoffs, Woolen registered four more pass breakups with eight total tackles.

2026 snap splits

Wide corner: 85.6%
Box: 12.4%

On the snap-split front, Woolen has a grand total of seven total snaps in the box, on the defensive line, and at free safety. For all intents and purposes, he’s about as full-time of an outside corner as it gets in today’s NFL.

How he’d fit with Bills

Given his size, explosiveness, experience, and pass-breakup radius (arm length in the 97th percentile), Woolen is a fun fit on just about every team. The Seahawks had the NFL’s fifth-highest zone coverage rate in 2025 and had a Top 10 zone-coverage percentage in three of Woolen’s four seasons with the club. The Eagles are almost right smack dab in the middle of zone-coverage rate (15th) in these first six games.

Essentially, Woolen is best in an off-man, zone-coverage style defense, and while Jim Leonhard was known for a man-coverage philosophy, the Bills have the ninth-lowest man-coverage rate entering their bye week.

Woolen has had double-digit pass breakups in each of his first four seasons in the NFL, and that six-pick rookie year of 2022

This year in Philadelphia, he’s played in all six games and has defended four passes to go along with 24 tackles. On 30 targets in his coverage area, Woolen has allowed 16 catches for 206 yards with three touchdowns. He’s surrendered a completion rate over 59% on targets in his coverage area in just one season to date in the NFL.

In short, Woolen would fit schematically — if the Bills continue their zone-heavy ways — I just don’t know if there’s room for him to come in and start at outside corner.

Financial obligation for Bills to trade for him

2026 salary: $1.26M

If the Bills trade for Woolen after Week 9, they’d be on the hook for $630k in prorated 2026 base salary. He’s an impending free agent after this season, which simultaneously creates plenty of flexibility for the Bills if he were to be in their future plans and lowers his asking price.

Projected cost to acquire

Using Syndicate32.com’s trade machine, the projected cost to trade for Woolen is an early Round 4 pick in 2027.

That feels just right for a player of Woolen’s caliber, at his age, and with his contract situation. He’s demonstrated big-play ability in his past but hasn’t been able to recreate the magic from his rookie season in 2022.

Should the Bills trade for Tariq Woolen?

If the Bills feel they desperately need to add an outside cornerback to the defense, Woolen should be at or near the top of their trade-candidate list at that position.

With Christian Benford, Davison Igbinosun, and, yes, even Max Hairston (I’d be silly to quit on him at this juncture), I don’t necessarily see how swinging a deal for a starting-caliber outside cornerback would be something the Bills brass would believe is a necessity right now.

Yet, given his expiring contract, the fact he should be in the prime of his NFL career, and what should be a relatively low acquisition cost, I could be talked into Woolen as a trade-deadline target simply because it’d give the Bills more talent in the secondary. His 70-plus games of NFL experience is very enticing too, especially relative to the youth in Buffalo’s cornerback room right now.

If the Bills can pry Woolen away from Howie Roseman and the Eagles for a fourth or fifth-round pick, I’d view the towering, incredibly fast and lengthy cornerback as a fine addition to Buffalo.

If he’s brought in, the Bills would have plus depth in their outside cornerback room.

item.title: Bears send a message to the NFL with the win over Patriots
item.description: The Bears picked up a key win over the Patriots on Thursday, and @jacobinfante24 shares his notes from the game.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears got the job done on Thursday night, defeating the New England Patriots 30-24 to improve their record to 5-2 for the season. It was a particularly strong performance from their offense, as Caleb Williams threw for 308 yards and two passing touchdowns in the victory.

In the four games that Williams has played, the Bears are 3-1. In the three of those games that weren’t played in the pouring rain, the Bears are 3-0. We haven’t seen much of this team at full strength, but when they have been there, the results have been extremely promising.

Even with a short week against a tough opponent, the Bears were able to pick up the win, and they now have a few extra days of rest leading into their Week 8 matchup against the Seattle Seahawks. For this week, though, these are some of my takeaways from the game.

Another high-powered offensive performance

Going back to the “when Caleb Williams is healthy” bit, the Bears are now averaging 40.0 points per game in the three healthy, non-monsoon games that he has played in 2026. Granted, that’s partially swayed by the Panthers game in which the offense put up 59 points, but Chicago is still coming off of consecutive games in which its offense scored 30 or more points, as well as consecutive games in which Williams threw for over 300 yards with multiple touchdowns and no interceptions.

It feels weird to say, but it feels like the Bears genuinely have an elite quarterback. After Thursday night, Williams ranks No. 4 in the entire NFL with an 84.2 PFN QB Impact grade. He’s surrounded by one of the brightest offensive minds in football, and he has plenty of talent on the offensive line and in the skill positions surrounding him. Against a solid defense in the Patriots, the Bears were incredibly effective. Thursday was just another instance of this team showing why it has one of the best offenses in the game.

The Jaylon Johnson conversation

Involving personal bias, it hurts to talk about Jaylon Johnson in a negative light. He was a rare bright spot on so many bad Bears teams, and he’s finally getting the chance to experience team success with the organization that drafted him back in 2020. By all accounts, he seems like a great guy. That said, his performance so far in 2026 is unacceptable for the massive salary he’s currently making.

So far this year, Johnson is allowing a targeted completion percentage of 71.4% and a targeted passer rating of 113.1 for the Bears. He looks a step slower coming out of his breaks than what we saw from him in his All-Pro campaign in 2023, as well as his Pro Bowl season in 2024. Additionally, he had two major whiffs as a tackler against the Patriots, including the last-second receiving touchdown by Rhamondre Stevenson, which saw him waltz into the end zone thanks to passive coverage by Chicago’s secondary and bad tackling by multiple players, including Johnson. Unless he can bounce back to his prior form, it’s starting to feel like the beginning of the end of his time with the team.

The ceiling of this Bears team

Negativity around that one subject aside, this was a massive win for the Bears. The Patriots were a red-hot team who had won three games in a row going into Week 7, and Chicago managed to shut them down and pick up the win. Now sitting at 5-2, this group is well-positioned for a playoff push and contention for first place in the NFC North, even with how talented the division is currently.

The Bears’ offense is operating at an incredibly high level. Their defense is manufacturing pressure up front with creative blitz looks and is still generating turnovers. I think it would really benefit the team to pursue a trade for a top defender before the 2026 trade deadline, as weaknesses at defensive tackle and cornerback still stand out. Even so, this Bears team is one that has proven it can take on top competition and be victorious. They could be a dark horse to make a deep playoff push when it’s all said and done.

item.title: 6 NFL trades we want to see at the deadline, including a Bears blockbuster
item.description: Trade targets with connective tissue to certain teams.
item.content:encoded:
We are a mere two weeks away from the mid-way point of the NFL season because time is a make-believe construct placed upon us by the man, which I believe is one of the reasons why the people of France are protesting.

The trade deadline is the Tuesday after Week 9, and there will be players on the move within the next handful of weeks. But rather than just throw names and teams into a random generator and tell you why they would be a fit, how about we make actual connections – both in terms of fit and previous relationships that could lure teams to players currently on the trade market.

WR Brian Thomas Jr to the New York Giants

Thomas has as many catches as you and I over his last two games, and it’s clear that he is at the bottom of the totem pole. This stems from last season when Thomas missed time due to injury. Jacksonville traded for Jakobi Meyers, and gave him a three-year, $60 million extension after a hot start with his new team all while Parker Washington was blooming into a star receiver. Washington has remained the team’s top target with Meyers as the No. 2. Thomas isn’t even the No. 3 option, though. Or the No. 4. Or the No. 5. Tight end Brenton Strange is tied for the team lead with 26 catches, and Josh Cameron has out-snapped Thomas over the last two games. Plus, Travis Hunter had a potential breakout game on both offense and defense in Week 6 against the Texans. It’s a matter of when Thomas gets traded, not if he will.

So why the Giants, you may ask. Well, they have a big need at receiver. Outside of Malik Nabers, their next-leading wide receiver is Malachi Fields with 12 catches. Thomas would instantly become the No. 2 receiver on the depth chart. To continue, the New York Giants’ wide receivers coach is Chad Hall, who was Thomas’ position coach in 2024 with the Jaguars when he put up nearly 1,300 yards and was a Pro Bowler as a rookie. And I’m sure that Nabers and Thomas would love to run back their LSU days playing side-by-side.

Not to ramble on about this one trade in particular, but it would also help the Giants win a wide open division, but also evaluate J.J. McCarthy and Jaxson Dart. Everyone loves Dart, but he spends more time in the blue tend then under center. If Thomas comes in and helps the Giants’ offense look good and win games under McCarthy, the Giants enter next spring with a quarterback battle on their hands. Having a pair of weapons like Nabers and Thomas would make it much easier to see who the best of the two quarterbacks is, and elevate whomever the starter ends up being.

WR Stefon Diggs to the Pittsburgh Steelers

The writing is on the wall for the Commanders. They’re 1-4-1, although Dan Quinn probably thinks they are 2-3-1. Jayden Daniels’ health, and overall demeanor are becoming real issues that have real question marks.

Steelers fans would likely prefer the younger Thomas, but assuming he ends up in New York, Diggs could be a name to whom they shift their attention.

Yes, he will turn 33 at the end of November, but Diggs is coming off a 1,000-yard season and playing good football for Washington. Through six weeks, he has 24 receptions and four touchdowns. 62.3 percent of his snaps have come from the slot this season, which could lead to the Steelers going with DK Metcalf and Germie Bernard on the outside with Diggs inside as their top three receivers, while also rotating in Michael Pittman and Roman Wilson.

To make a similar connection to that of Thomas and Chad Hall, Steelers wide receivers coach Adam Henry was with Diggs in Buffalo in 2023 – a year in which Diggs caught 107 passes.

EDGE Josh Sweat to Green Bay Packers

This one is pretty cut and dry. Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon coached Sweat when he was the head coach in Arizona. When Micah Parsons returns, a pairing of he and Sweat would give the Packers a tremendous duo off the edge that would help supplement the loss of Edgerrin Cooper.

S Derwin James to Dallas Cowboys

The Chargers are a tire fire and should immediately begin a fire sale with James at the top of the list.

As fun as it would be to see James reunite with Jesse Minter in Baltimore to play alongside Kyle Hamilton, the two safeties share a lot of similar responsibilities defensively, so I’ll go with the Cowboys, whose defense continues to give up big play after big play. Dallas has already traded for cornerback Joey Porter Jr, and if there is one thing Jerry Jones isn’t afraid to do, it’s make moves if it gives Dallas a better chance at winning.

The connection for James to Dallas is Derrick Ansley, who is the Cowboys’ defensive backs coach and served as the defensive backs coach with the Chargers from 2021-22 and their defensive coordinator in 2023. This is a Cowboys team that has started very slow due to inconsistencies in large part on defense, and a proven All-Pro like James could help clean up some of those issues.

EDGE Khalil Mack to Buffalo Bills

The connection to Mack isn’t on the coaching staff, but in the city itself. He is a Buffalo native and went to the University of Buffalo. Considering the nine-time Pro Bowler has yet to appear in a Super Bowl, going back home and playing alongside Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb could help both he and the Bills get over the hump.

RB Jonathan Taylor to Chicago Bears

This would be a case of the rich getting richer. The Bears’ offense is already incredibly dynamic, and the Colts are floundering after a loss to the Titans. They fired GM Chris Ballard, and head coach Shane Steichen could be next sooner than later.

The Bears making a play for Jonathan Taylor would remind me a lot of the 49ers trading for Christian McCaffrey. Granted, Chicago has yet to reach a Super Bowl, but they also have a better quarterback than the 49ers did at the time of the McCaffrey trade. Putting Taylor behind Caleb Williams would give the Bears a bump in the run game, which they currently rank 16th in success rate.

The connection is a bit of a reach, admittedly, but current offensive coordinator Press Taylor was an offensive assistant with the Colts in 2021, the year Taylor ran for over 1,800 yards and 18 touchdowns. Seeing what he and Ben Johnson would do in the run game with Taylor is something we all deserve to see, and they could be a sneaky team that makes a big move for the All-Pro running back.

item.title: Stampede Blue Reacts results (Week 7): Colts fans show signs of optimism after Ballard firing
item.description: The latest SB Nation Reacts survey suggests Colts fans may not be ready to give up on the 2026 season just yet.
item.content:encoded:
According to this week’s results, 47 percent of Colts fans say they are confident the team is headed in the right direction. That number is still far from overwhelming, and it shows that a large portion of the fan base remains unconvinced, but it is also a notable sign that optimism has not completely disappeared in Indianapolis.

Just a few days ago, fan confidence felt like it had hit a breaking point following the Colts’ embarrassing collapse against the previously winless Tennessee Titans. Indianapolis looked firmly in control early, built a 13-0 halftime lead and still found a way to lose 26-20 in one of the most frustrating performances of the season. For many fans, it felt like another example of the same problems that have defined this era of Colts football: inconsistency, missed opportunities and an inability to take advantage of games the team should win.

Then came the major change! Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon fired general manager Chris Ballard less than 24 hours after the loss, ending a tenure that had increasingly become a source of frustration for much of the fan base. Ballard’s dismissal does not fix the roster overnight, and it does not erase the disappointing start to the season, but it clearly signaled a willingness from ownership to make a significant change rather than continue down the same path. That alone may have helped restore at least some belief that the franchise is capable of moving in a different direction.

The 47 percent confidence mark reflects a fan base that is still conflicted. Colts fans are frustrated, and understandably so, but there also appears to be some renewed hope that meaningful change could lead to better days ahead. If Shane Steichen’s team can string together a few wins and climb back into the playoff picture, confidence could rise quickly. If not, this number could just as easily fall again.

For now, though, nearly half of Colts fans still believe this franchise may be headed in the right direction.

Elsewhere around the NFL, fans were also asked which head coach they believe will be the first fired this season, and Colts head coach Shane Steichen received 17% of the vote, tied with Tampa Bay’s Todd Bowles for second place behind Washington’s Dan Quinn (34%). Steichen’s inclusion should come as little surprise given Indianapolis’ disappointing start to the season and the recent dismissal of Chris Ballard. While ownership has already made one major organizational change, Steichen remains under considerable pressure to turn things around, particularly with the Colts still fighting to remain in the AFC playoff picture. A few victories over the coming weeks could go a long way toward improving his job security, but another extended losing streak could leave ownership facing another difficult decision before the season is over.

item.title: Scouting the Enemy: Arizona Cardinals
item.description: The Denver Broncos battle the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. Here is a deeper look at their Week 7 opponent.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos will finish up their slate of NFC West games on Sunday when they head on the road to face the Arizona Cardinals. The Cardinals are 2-4 entering this matchup, but are coming off an impressive Week 6 win against the Los Angeles Rams. Here ia deeper look at Denver’s Week 7 opponent.

2025 Arizona Cardinals Regular Season Review

The Cardinals finished their 2025 regular season with 3-14 record and were last place in the NFC West. That led to the firing of Head Coach Jonathan Gannon after three seasons with the team. He was replaced by Mike LaFleur.

2026 Arizona Cardinals Offseason Additions and Departures

When coaching regimes change, rosters also change. The Cardinals made a lot of moves this past off-season and are clearly trying to establish a different culture and identity.

On offense, there were two significant departures. They moved on from quarterback Kyler Murray and recently traded wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Houston Texans. On defense, they parted ways with defensive linemen Dalvin Tomlinson and Bilal Nichols and linebacker Akeem-Davis Gaither.

In free agency, they signed Gardner Minshew to be Jacoby Brissett’s backup. They revamped their receiving corps adding Kendrick Bourne, Devin Duvernay, and Simi Fehoko. Tyler Allgeier was a big signing to bolster their ground game, and they added several starters to their offensive and defensive trenches.

In the 2026 NFL Draft, the Cardinals took Notre Dame standout Jeremiyah Love to help be a foundational piece of their offense. In the second round, the drafted Texas A&M guard Chase Bisontis. Unfortunately, he tore his MCL in the preseason and is out for the year. Georgia quarterback Carson Beck was their third round selection. Overall, they haven’t had a big impact from their rookie class.

Offensive X-Factor: Tight end Trey McBride

The focal point of the Cardinals passing attack is fifth-year tight end Trey McBride. He is one of the NFL’s best tight ends. I feel he is easily the biggest X-Factor for Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph and his players to try to combat on Sunday.

McBride is coming off a remarkable 2025 season where he had 126 catches, 1,239 receiving yards, and 11 touchdowns. That incredible production earned him first-team All-Pro honors. This season, he leads the NFL with 49 catches in six games. However, his decline in yards per catch is drastic, with just 361 yards on those receptions with 3 touchdowns.

For the most part, Denver’s defense has done quite well limiting the top receiving option for opposing teams through six games. In order to win on Sunday, they can’t let McBride have a big game. He will be targeted often and has a penchant for moving the chains on third down. Limit his impact and things should look good for the Broncos.

Defensive X-Factor: Defensive back Budda Baker

The Cardinals have struggled on defense this season. However, one player in particular stands out above the rest on their roster. That’s defensive back Budda Baker. Since being selected in the second-round of the 2017 NFL Draft, Baker has been a mainstay in the Cardinals’ defensive backfield.

He is an eight-time Pro Bowler and a four-time All-Pro. Some of the best seasons of his career were when Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph was calling the shots for their defense. A decade later, Baker continues to be an impact player for their defense due to his versatility.

In his tenth season, Baker already has 42 tackles, 4 tackles for loss, 3.5 sacks, 5 quarterback hits, and 1 interception. He is a do-it-all player that can make a huge impact in Sunday’s matchup. The Cardinals run a lot of Cover 3 looks and he has a nose for the football. Despite his size, he is quite tenacious in run support and does well executing his run fits.

In pass coverage, the veteran defensive back has taken a bit of a step back this year. While he has allowed just 13 of 25 targets in his direction to be completed (52-percent), those completions have gone for 197 yards three of those have been touchdowns. Even so, I still think he is the player Bo Nix and the offense needs to be the most cognizant about. He has had a remarkable career and has made a lot of big plays. Denver can’t let that happen on Sunday.

How the Broncos can achieve a victory over the Cardinals

Like most of Denver’s wins this season, they are going to need a great performance from their defense. The Broncos will need to dial up the heat and put pressure on Jacoby Brissett. I think Zach Allen is poised for a big game returning home to face the team who drafted him, and believe Jonathon Cooper can make a difference at edge rusher.

On offense, Denver needs Bo Nix to finally play a good game. Let’s see the aerial attack finally take flight. But in my opinion, this is a prime opportunity for their rushing offense to get going. The Cardinals are one of the worst defending the run. It’s time for Denver to run the ball with authority. That would help their offense significantly.

Hart’s Prediction: Broncos 27, Cardinals 16.

item.title: Missed tackles tell the story of the Patriots’ loss to the Bears
item.description: New England missed 16 tackles in Thursday’s loss
item.content:encoded:
After missing eight tackles in a gritty win over the New York Jets last week, the New England Patriots doubled that total on Thursday night, missing 16 tackles in a 30-24 defeat to the Chicago Bears.

The last time the Patriots eclipsed that total?

Look no further than their 29-13 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in Super Bowl LX, where New England trailed 19-0 in the fourth quarter.

“[Our] tackling wasn’t good enough. Not against his team,” head coach Mike Vrabel said. “We knew coming in, certainly tackling on Thursday night, but against this team, whether it’s [D’Andre] Swift, [Luther Burden III] or [Caleb Williams], it just leads to extra yards and conversions. But we fought, and I would say that we need to turn the ball over and we have to tackle better, and those are fundamental skills.”

Struggling to consistently match the Bears’ physicality past the line of scrimmage, the Patriots’ defense had difficulty shedding blocks, which played a significant role in Luther Burden III’s 130 yards and one touchdown on just four catches in the first half alone.

That mismatch remained in the second half.

Early in the third quarter, the Chicago offense ran a naked bootleg 11 yards out from the end zone. Caleb Williams connected with his tight end, Colston Loveland, crossing over the middle of the field. Loveland, turning towards the end zone, quickly shed a Marcus Jones tackle and fought through another two New England defenders as he broke past the plane to extend the Patriots’ deficit by two scores.

“I got to make the tackle when it comes down to that,” Jones said. “And then [the Bears] had certain schemes where they would line up in certain formations, run overs to where we’re away from leverage and things like that. But as the game went on, we learned and stuff, but I’m a hard critic of myself. So, I will get it corrected for sure.”

On the ground, the story wasn’t much different.

With Swift and a handful of Roschon Johnson carries, Chicago managed 3.1 yards after contact in the run game against New England’s defensive front. That number surpasses the Kansas City Chiefs’ league-leading average of three yards per attempt this season with Kenneth Walker.

The defensive line’s shortcomings in finishing plays also extended into its pass rush. Although the Patriots sacked Williams three times, the unit generated 25 total pressures on his dropbacks and created plenty more opportunities to force Williams into inaccurate throws. Too often, however, the opposing quarterback escaped near-sacks and turned those plays into chunk gains through the air.

Williams threw for 308 yards and two touchdowns on the evening, completing 22 of his 33 pass attempts. Meanwhile, New England’s defense came up short in its efforts to force a turnover.

“We talked about it all week. [Williams is] very gifted with how he can run and how he can extend plays,” cornerback Christian Gonzalez said. “I talked about before the game: you got to defend the second play. There’s a play, and then there’s a second play with a quarterback like Caleb. So, it’s a challenge for the secondary. It’s about the whole team, but we look forward to it. We embrace it, and they got the best of us tonight.”

item.title: Carolina Panthers 2026 fan mailbag: Injury woes, scoring points, safety room, and more!
item.description: Answering all your questions in this week’s fan mailbag!
item.content:encoded:
Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! I’m here to answer all your questions from earlier in the week, whether they be Panthers related, football related, or even completely off topic! Let’s dive right in to all your questions!

kevinjalltheway: The Eagles still had a very good defense. If we had wanted to, we could have made it a 2 touchdown win at least with a field goal, let alone powered it in for another touchdown and a 18 point margin of victory. Points scored do matter in playoff scenarios right? I believe I remember years ago when we were competing with the Packers for a playoff spot and we were piling up points on the Buc’s (?) as Green Bay was piling up points against whoever they were playing and we were scoreboard watching.

Its very rare that points scored factors into anything, usually the head to head matchups end up being the tie breakers for playoff scenarios in the wild card. I also think with how beaten up this offensive line has been, just getting out of there with the win made a lot of sense. I’m not concerned at all with the decision, and we don’t have to deal with the same hate as fans we had for Sean Payton for running up the score.

@WTMealey: BY5K?

He’s certainly on pace for it. The Panthers still have a long schedule ahead of them and an injury or two to the receiving options makes that harder. So my official answer is, improbable, but not impossible.

schrodingersblackcat: You’re suddenly and inexplicably teleported to the opposing team’s pass rush. Would you rather try to get past Tremble or Hubbard?

Chuba Hubbard is a great pass blocker for a running back, but I’m definitely not trying to square up with Tommy Tremble in this scenario. Dude already entered the league as a great blocker and his receiving skills have developed over time.

brake23: The safety room has become very interesting. Zakee Wheatley is beginning to emerge as a clear starter moving forward and played 81% of the snaps on Sunday. However, I noticed Ransom to be missing. I thought that he and Chau Smith-Wade’s snaps would have went up with Jaycee and MJ out. Smith-Wade had 2 snaps on defense and Ransom only had 1!!! Is this a result of bad play from either one of them or is Evero just obsessed with sticking with Nick Scott and now Akayleb Evans? I guess this speaks volumes on how he feels about Wheatley being in most of the game as a rookie and essentially benching Ransom.

Lathan Ransom’s skillset mirrors that of Tre’Von Moehrig, so I think its more about fielding a diversified skillset rather than having preferences or one guy playing worse than another. Nick Scott is still their deep middle safety, but I think Zakee Wheatley will eventually take that role from him now that we’re seeing consistency. Ejiro Evero has very specific roles in his defenses and he’s fitting the pieces in. Akayleb Evans having a large amount of snaps is puzzling, but I am willing to let Evero cook after a fantastic showing against the Eagles by the entire secondary.

sgtx: Hey Brian, The Panthers are riding high and I don’t know how to feel? Help me out.

I feel things. I am not sure what they are. But feeling things is better than feeling nothing, which was the norm since the end of the 2010s.

DeacCat: Do we need to be concerned that Jaeden Phillips has (I think) only seven tackles in the last four games?

Oysters: Raw, Roasted, Steamed, Other?

Jaelan Phillips has shown more of an impact simply being on the field than he has as a pass rusher from a statistical standpoint. He collapses the pocket, sets the edge, and pursues in both the rushing and passing game extremely well. His presence opens up the rest of the defense for better matchups and paths in their gaps and pass rushing lanes. Certainly concerning he has been injured, but when he’s in the game, he’s been worth every penny.

I am definitely a raw oysters guy. There’s just nothing like it, and a versatile dish. That said, I’m pretty much okay with any style of oyster. Sound off on your favorites in the comments!

hollywud: Since someone brought up our safeties, How would you view Tre’von Moehrig’s play this year overall? He doesn’t get mentioned much but seems to be Evero’s chess piece in the defensive scheme.

Once Evero started using him as more of a pseudo-linebacker last year, he’s been excellent. His strengths have always been as a blitzer and in run support, and the way Evero deploys him allows them to use guys like Zakee Wheatley, Lathan Ransom, and Nick Scott in more complimentary roles. I think Zakee Wheatley is the big benefactor of having someone like Tre on the field, because he does a lot of things that Wheatley doesn’t excel at. They are building a nice little stable of safeties.

Coach_K: Trade deadline not til Nov 10th, but stories/speculation is increasing this week as more players are being waived. Cornerback will be spotlighted no doubt. But how about the running back position? Heard Jonathan Brooks is getting close to coming back, at least jogging. Do you think we’ll bolster that RB position regardless? For instance, saw Najee Harris was let go the other day. It seems like it’s always been for us to have two running backs to share the ball

The Panthers seem content shuffling their group of running backs as the rest of the guys behind Chuba Hubbard get healthy. They brought back Trevor Etienne and he had a role this week. I don’t expect them to make any major moves on RB unless Chuba becomes unavailable for an extended period. Probably looking at more of a waiver wire or free agency transaction than a trade.

SnarkyComet: Which injured player do you think we’re missing the most right now? Not necessarily our best player who’s out, but if you had a magic wand and could heal any player and insert them directly into the roster, whose return would make the biggest difference given where the team stands today?

Probably Jaycee Horn by a country mile, and that’s no slight on anyone else who is injured. There was a clear plan for Horn to man the middle as their nickel corner while still playing outside, he was another chess piece Evero intended to move around as needed. Horn can do it all, he can even blitz extremely well when called upon. I think this defense would be in much better shape if Will Lee was only filling in for Mike Jackson rather than being the number one corner by default. But EDGE Nic Scourton is a very close second, I think this pass rush would be much better rushing four guys if Scourton was fully healthy.

SnarkyComet: Looking at the Bucs’ record and the fact that we’re road favorites again this week, it’s easy to feel pretty good about this matchup. But it’s also a divisional rivalry, and we all know how quickly those games can defy expectations. So, what does a Panthers loss look like on Sunday? What are the biggest things Carolina needs to avoid to make sure we come away with a win?

The Bucs defense, especially against the run, is underrated. If the Panthers are forced to be one dimensional on offense or simply can’t keep on schedule, that creates a recipe for a very close game that’s won by only one or two big key plays. And the Panthers just can’t stop getting flagged for penalties. They need to come out swinging fast to win this one, in my opinion.

That’s all for this week Panthers fans! Enjoy Game Day, and KEEP POUNDING!!

item.title: The next two weeks will determine Shane Steichen’s future with the Colts
item.description: The Colts coach is in trouble if he doesn’t produce some quick wins.
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts made a major decision when the Irsays chose to part ways with 10-year general manager Chris Ballard. It was a long time coming, but if things don’t shape up quickly, it won’t be the last move made in 2026. When it rains, it pours, and Shane Steichen better have his umbrella and poncho on because he is in danger of being the next to fall. The next two weeks could very well determine his fate. 

Offensively, the 5-0 Minnesota Vikings are one of the worst undefeated teams ever. They don’t put up a lot of yards or points. That’s all the good news there is for the Colts, though. As statistically bad as they may be on offense, they are coming off a bye, are at home, and have one of the league’s best defenses. Kyler Murray is back under center and is starting to get comfortable. In the building in which the Colts surrendered a 33-0 lead, anything is possible, but being a touchdown underdog implies this will be an uphill climb.

If Steichen can rally the troops in the face of adversity and win, he can take a breath. It will only be a small gulp, however, because the test continues in Jacksonville against the Jaguars. Their record doesn’t matter. Whether Trevor Lawrence has his team rolling doesn’t matter. Great or horrible, the Colts don’t win in Jacksonville anymore. If Steichen wants to keep his job, this has to be the year to break the curse.

These are two tough games to get the mojo back. Shane Steichen can script the first twenty or so plays, but after that, it falls apart. The Colts have already shown what “Find a Way” means when they released Ballard. It means win. Nothing else. Steichen’s leash was short to begin the year, and he is officially on notice as the next one on the chopping block. If he loses both, he will most likely be gone. This is a results-oriented league. Steichen must show those results or be shown the door.
